* fix: narrow every label_manager remove list, and stop failures reading as "no labels"

`removable()` exists because `gh issue edit --remove-label X` errors when the *repo*
has no label X at all -- not just when the issue lacks it -- and a fresh target repo
only has the labels something already created, so the whole edit fails, add included.
It was applied to park, unpark and clear-attempts. `spec`, `attempt` and `merge-ready`
kept building their remove lists unconditionally.

Two of the three are on paths the driver takes on every run, and both swallow the
failure:

    parking.py:82   increment_attempts -> `attempt --count N`   except Exception: pass
    parking.py:369  apply_park_state   -> `merge-ready`         except Exception: pass

So on a fresh target repo the attempt counter silently never increments -- and the
attempt counter is the thing that stops a phase looping forever -- while the
gate-eligible success path silently fails to stamp merge-ready.

The test file's own header diagnosed this in full ("There were no tests here at all
before this file, which is why three commands carried the same bug") and then covered
only the three commands that got the fix. Eight new tests, written against the existing
FakeGh, fail with the exact production error before the change.

Second half, in scope because the first half widened its reach.
`get_current_labels` did `except Exception: return []`, making a rate limit, a 401 and a
genuinely unlabelled issue indistinguishable -- while every caller reads the result as
fact. `validate_transition` derives `is_parked` from it, so an empty list means "not
parked" and the guard permits re-speccing or re-attempting a parked issue. And now that
all six commands narrow through `removable`, an empty list would also silently skip
removals. Both are a null rendering as a positive.

It now propagates, and `main` catches it before touching anything: exit 1, a message
naming the issue, and no edit attempted. The driver's callers already wrap these in
`except Exception`, so they degrade to a no-op rather than a wrong action.

`ensure_label_exists` likewise narrowed from a bare `except RuntimeError: pass` to the
already-exists case, so a 403 from a read-only token no longer looks like success.

Refs #261 (C1, C9).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor: give the driver's output and clock a home, breaking the barrel cycle

`agent_session_driver.py` was a 143-line re-export barrel that defined nothing, and the
package reached back through it constantly: 14 function-local imports across `lifecycle`,
`board`, `parking` and `locks`, existing purely to break the cycle the barrel created.

Two distinct things were tangled in there.

**Five spellings of one output helper set.** `say` defined four times, `log` twice, `die`
twice. Three were byte-identical; `board`'s three were trampolines that went through the
barrel to arrive at `lifecycle`'s copies. Writing one line to stdout could take three hops
through an import cycle, and which implementation you got depended on which module you
were in.

**The barrel was also the clock**, and this is the part worth stating plainly, because it
is easy to mistake for a vestige: eight call sites across five modules read
`agent_session_driver.datetime`, not because they wanted the barrel but because patching
that single attribute freezes time everywhere at once. The full-loop suite depends on it
for byte-stable `runs.jsonl` rows. That is a real and useful seam -- it was just housed in
a module whose only job was re-exporting, so every module that needed the clock had to
import the barrel from inside a function body.

New `output.py`: `say`, `log`, `die`, and `now()` as the named clock. It imports nothing
from `agent_sessions.driver`, which is what lets everything else import it at module
scope. All eight clock reads and all five output-helper definitions now route through it.

Result: function-local barrel imports drop from 14 across four modules to 7 across two --
`board.py` and `locks.py` are out of the cycle entirely. The barrel no longer re-exports
`datetime`/`timezone`, and its docstring now says what it is (an entry point that defines
nothing) and where the code actually lives, which is the single most likely thing to send
a new contributor to the wrong file.

Also removes `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))` from the barrel -- a
pre-package fossil that put the package directory itself on sys.path, making `board`,
`locks`, `gate`, `router` and `credentials` importable as bare top-level names. Nothing
needed it; every import in that file is absolute. Verified the launcher still resolves.

Two test patches had to move, and both were the same latent defect as the
CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE one fixed earlier in this branch -- patching a re-exported name:

- `test_full_loop` froze time via `setattr(agent_session_driver, "datetime", ...)`; it now
  replaces `output.now`, which is one setattr on the module that owns the clock.
- `test_driver` captured log lines via `setattr(...agent_session_driver.log, ...)`, which
  worked only because `board.log` was a call-time trampoline. It now patches `board.log`.

Refs #261 (T1 partial, part of T4, part of D9).

* refactor: import the output helpers instead of re-exporting them

Les caught this on review: `say = output.say` with a comment saying it exists
"because `agent_session_driver` and the tests import them from this module". He
asked whether that implies fixing the importers instead. It does, and the comment
was partly false.

Measured:

- **No test imports them from anywhere.** That half of the justification was
  invented. `test_driver.py` in fact documents the opposite — it patches
  `board.log` directly, with a comment explaining that patching a re-export
  "no longer reaches it, the same shape as the CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE patch that
  silently did nothing."
- **The facade did import them, from `lifecycle`**, and re-exported them in
  `__all__`, and **nothing anywhere consumed the result.** So the alias existed to
  feed a re-export that fed nobody.
- **`pr_checks.py` aliased `say` and never called it.** Purely dead.

So the chain was `output.say` -> alias in `lifecycle` -> facade imports it *from
lifecycle* -> `__all__` -> no consumer.

What it bought was a trap. A re-export of a function is a bound copy, so
`monkeypatch.setattr(agent_session_driver, "log", ...)` reads as patching the
emitter and patches nothing — which is precisely the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` defect
this branch fixes two commits earlier. Leaving `say`/`log`/`die` on the facade set
the same trap for the next person.

Now:

- `board`, `lifecycle` and `parking` bind them with a real
  `from agent_sessions.driver.output import ...`. Same brevity — `lifecycle` calls
  `say` 55 times — and `lifecycle.say` stays patchable the way the suites already
  patch `board.log`. It just no longer pretends to be a re-export.
- `pr_checks` drops the dead alias.
- The facade stops importing and exporting them, and its docstring says why.

**The clock is deliberately different.** `output.now()` stays a module-qualified
call everywhere, because a bound copy could not be frozen, and freezing it is how
the suites get deterministic timestamps. That asymmetry is now stated where it
could otherwise look like an inconsistency.

A guard pins it: nothing may put `say`/`log`/`die` back into the facade's `__all__`.
Mutation-tested — adding one back fails it. Worth asserting because the re-export is
one line and reads as harmless.

* refactor: import the output helper in locks too, and check for the rest

Les spotted `log = output.log` still in `locks.py`. It is the same remnant the
previous commit removed from five other modules, and I missed it.

`locks.py` used `output` for nothing else, so the module import goes with it.
Nothing patches `locks.log`, so there is no seam to preserve.

The reason this gets a check rather than a second tidy-up is the miss itself. The
alias and a real import bind the same object, so nothing failed and nothing could
fail — the difference is only in what the line *claims*. An assignment reads as
"this module provides `log`", which invites patching it, and patching it reaches a
copy. That is the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` trap, in the file where
`CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` lives.

One line, easy to add without thinking, invisible to every existing check, and I
grepped for it by hand and still left one. So: an AST check over the driver package
for a module-level `<name> = output.<name>`. Mutation-tested — putting the alias
back in `locks.py` fails it, naming the file and line.

`output.now()` is deliberately outside the ban and inside the check's reach. It has
to stay module-qualified so the suites can freeze the clock, and a `now = output.now`
alias is precisely what would silently break that. If one appears, this catches it.

* fix: install the merge-block hook again, and fail closed when it cannot be

The PreToolUse hook that denies `gh pr merge`, `gh api PUT .../pulls/N/merge` and the
`curl` equivalent has not been installed on any fresh state dir since the 2026-08-09
Python conversion. `lifecycle.preflight` resolved its two assets as
`Path(__file__).parent / ...` while they sat in repo-root `driver/`, so the
`if template.is_file():` guard skipped the render, nothing was written, and
`invoke_agent` went on passing `--settings <path that was never written>`.

It looked fine locally because `.driver-state/settings.json` is an Aug 6
pre-conversion leftover that happens to point at a real script. The decafclaw state
dir's copy points into a worktree that no longer exists.

Three things, in the order they matter:

1. The assets move into `src/agent_sessions/driver/`, beside the module that loads
   them. Verified the wheel ships them (hatch already includes non-Python files under
   the package). `driver/` now holds exactly the compatibility launcher, which is the
   coherent end state of the conversion.

2. The render fails closed. `render_hook_settings` dies on a missing, non-executable
   or unreadable asset instead of skipping. A safety control that silently omits
   itself when its asset is absent is worse than one that is missing, because nothing
   reports the difference -- that is the whole reason this survived.

3. The tests grade the code instead of the artifact. The three previous tests never
   touched the install path: one asserted a string appeared in `lifecycle.py`'s source
   text, one loaded the template by repo-relative literal and checked its shape, and
   one shelled out to `jq` to redo the substitution and asserted that jq works. They
   all passed throughout. Replaced with tests that call `preflight` and assert the
   rendered file exists, targets Bash, and names an executable that exists -- plus a
   control proving a missing template now stops the run.

`backend_permission_probe` no longer re-implements the substitution; it delegates to
`render_hook_settings`. Its own copy was the only correct resolver while the driver's
was wrong, so the probe attested to a hook no real run installed.

Also adds `git push -f` to both backends' deny lists -- the short form matched
nothing, since only `git push --force` was spelled out. Deliberately *not* adding
tool-level rules for the REST merge paths: those patterns would have to match
mid-command, `--help` does not state whether the rule syntax supports that, and an
unverified entry in a floor whose value is that it is verified is the wrong trade.
The hook covers them, now per-vector tested, and `make backend-permission-probe` is
the one live run that would settle the syntax question.

Updates the claims this move falsified: the `driver/**` allowlist clause in both
governance files now says plainly that it grants nothing, and `orientation.md`'s
layout bullets and file table point at the real locations. Its prose restatement of
the allowlist is deleted rather than corrected -- it had already drifted by omitting
`tests/**`, which is what the no-duplicate-live-sources rule exists to prevent.

Refs #261 (S1, S2, part of D3, H4).

* test: stop the suites writing into the operator's home directory

There was no conftest.py anywhere in the repo, so nothing pinned XDG_STATE_HOME.
`lifecycle.preflight` derives its state dir from that variable (falling back to
$HOME/.local/state) plus `agent-session/<repo-with-dashes>`, and the fixture repo is
`owner/repo` -- so every test that drove the driver without passing --state-dir wrote
to a real path in $HOME. Measured before this change:

still growing, with rows timestamped during this session's own test runs.

The worst consequence is not disk. `make evidence` reads a per-repo runs.jsonl, and
the fix for it currently reading a superseded archive is to point it at the live state
root -- at which point 1748 fabricated rows become "evidence" about runs that never
happened. So this has to land first.

--state-dir and asserts the result lands inside tmp_path, plus a polarity case that
unsets the pin and confirms the fallback still resolves to the path that leaked.

it, which is how the original went unnoticed.

Second fixture, for the lock global. The full-loop harness had:

    monkeypatch.setattr(agent_session_driver, "CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE", None)
    # ... so no pass can leave a live lock behind

which did nothing -- that module binds a copy of the value at import while `locks`
mutates its own global through `global`, and nothing in src/ reads the re-exported
name. The symptom was visible on every single run: real `Releasing lock for #N...`
lines at pytest exit, the atexit hook firing after monkeypatch had restored the true
subprocess.run. Survivable only because the tmp_path repos have no `origin` to receive
a ref deletion.

Patched on the owning module, plus an autouse teardown that clears it.

Worth recording that the teardown started as an assertion that the global was already
None, and it failed at once on the full-loop passes -- correctly, because a pass that
acquires a lock and returns really does end holding it. That is the driver's designed
behaviour: the lock covers the process. Asserting against it would have been asserting
that the driver releases something it is built to keep, so the fixture resets and does
not assert. The reset is the part that removes the harm.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor: give the driver's output and clock a home, breaking the barrel cycle

`agent_session_driver.py` was a 143-line re-export barrel that defined nothing, and the
package reached back through it constantly: 14 function-local imports across `lifecycle`,
`board`, `parking` and `locks`, existing purely to break the cycle the barrel created.

Two distinct things were tangled in there.

**Five spellings of one output helper set.** `say` defined four times, `log` twice, `die`
twice. Three were byte-identical; `board`'s three were trampolines that went through the
barrel to arrive at `lifecycle`'s copies. Writing one line to stdout could take three hops
through an import cycle, and which implementation you got depended on which module you
were in.

**The barrel was also the clock**, and this is the part worth stating plainly, because it
is easy to mistake for a vestige: eight call sites across five modules read
`agent_session_driver.datetime`, not because they wanted the barrel but because patching
that single attribute freezes time everywhere at once. The full-loop suite depends on it
for byte-stable `runs.jsonl` rows. That is a real and useful seam -- it was just housed in
a module whose only job was re-exporting, so every module that needed the clock had to
import the barrel from inside a function body.

New `output.py`: `say`, `log`, `die`, and `now()` as the named clock. It imports nothing
from `agent_sessions.driver`, which is what lets everything else import it at module
scope. All eight clock reads and all five output-helper definitions now route through it.

Result: function-local barrel imports drop from 14 across four modules to 7 across two --
`board.py` and `locks.py` are out of the cycle entirely. The barrel no longer re-exports
`datetime`/`timezone`, and its docstring now says what it is (an entry point that defines
nothing) and where the code actually lives, which is the single most likely thing to send
a new contributor to the wrong file.

Also removes `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))` from the barrel -- a
pre-package fossil that put the package directory itself on sys.path, making `board`,
`locks`, `gate`, `router` and `credentials` importable as bare top-level names. Nothing
needed it; every import in that file is absolute. Verified the launcher still resolves.

Two test patches had to move, and both were the same latent defect as the
CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE one fixed earlier in this branch -- patching a re-exported name:

- `test_full_loop` froze time via `setattr(agent_session_driver, "datetime", ...)`; it now
  replaces `output.now`, which is one setattr on the module that owns the clock.
- `test_driver` captured log lines via `setattr(...agent_session_driver.log, ...)`, which
  worked only because `board.log` was a call-time trampoline. It now patches `board.log`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor: import the output helpers instead of re-exporting them

Les caught this on review: `say = output.say` with a comment saying it exists
"because `agent_session_driver` and the tests import them from this module". He
asked whether that implies fixing the importers instead. It does, and the comment
was partly false.

Measured:

- **No test imports them from anywhere.** That half of the justification was
  invented. `test_driver.py` in fact documents the opposite — it patches
  `board.log` directly, with a comment explaining that patching a re-export
  "no longer reaches it, the same shape as the CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE patch that
  silently did nothing."
- **The facade did import them, from `lifecycle`**, and re-exported them in
  `__all__`, and **nothing anywhere consumed the result.** So the alias existed to
  feed a re-export that fed nobody.
- **`pr_checks.py` aliased `say` and never called it.** Purely dead.

So the chain was `output.say` -> alias in `lifecycle` -> facade imports it *from
lifecycle* -> `__all__` -> no consumer.

What it bought was a trap. A re-export of a function is a bound copy, so
`monkeypatch.setattr(agent_session_driver, "log", ...)` reads as patching the
emitter and patches nothing — which is precisely the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` defect
this branch fixes two commits earlier. Leaving `say`/`log`/`die` on the facade set
the same trap for the next person.

Now:

- `board`, `lifecycle` and `parking` bind them with a real
  `from agent_sessions.driver.output import ...`. Same brevity — `lifecycle` calls
  `say` 55 times — and `lifecycle.say` stays patchable the way the suites already
  patch `board.log`. It just no longer pretends to be a re-export.
- `pr_checks` drops the dead alias.
- The facade stops importing and exporting them, and its docstring says why.

**The clock is deliberately different.** `output.now()` stays a module-qualified
call everywhere, because a bound copy could not be frozen, and freezing it is how
the suites get deterministic timestamps. That asymmetry is now stated where it
could otherwise look like an inconsistency.

A guard pins it: nothing may put `say`/`log`/`die` back into the facade's `__all__`.
Mutation-tested — adding one back fails it. Worth asserting because the re-export is
one line and reads as harmless.

* refactor: import the output helper in locks too, and check for the rest

Les spotted `log = output.log` still in `locks.py`. It is the same remnant the
previous commit removed from five other modules, and I missed it.

`locks.py` used `output` for nothing else, so the module import goes with it.
Nothing patches `locks.log`, so there is no seam to preserve.

The reason this gets a check rather than a second tidy-up is the miss itself. The
alias and a real import bind the same object, so nothing failed and nothing could
fail — the difference is only in what the line *claims*. An assignment reads as
"this module provides `log`", which invites patching it, and patching it reaches a
copy. That is the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` trap, in the file where
`CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` lives.

One line, easy to add without thinking, invisible to every existing check, and I
grepped for it by hand and still left one. So: an AST check over the driver package
for a module-level `<name> = output.<name>`. Mutation-tested — putting the alias
back in `locks.py` fails it, naming the file and line.

`output.now()` is deliberately outside the ban and inside the check's reach. It has
to stay module-qualified so the suites can freeze the clock, and a `now = output.now`
alias is precisely what would silently break that. If one appears, this catches it.

commit.message:
fix: install the merge-block hook again, and stop the suites writing into $HOME (#263)

* fix: install the merge-block hook again, and fail closed when it cannot be

The PreToolUse hook that denies `gh pr merge`, `gh api PUT .../pulls/N/merge` and the
`curl` equivalent has not been installed on any fresh state dir since the 2026-08-09
Python conversion. `lifecycle.preflight` resolved its two assets as
`Path(__file__).parent / ...` while they sat in repo-root `driver/`, so the
`if template.is_file():` guard skipped the render, nothing was written, and
`invoke_agent` went on passing `--settings <path that was never written>`.

It looked fine locally because `.driver-state/settings.json` is an Aug 6
pre-conversion leftover that happens to point at a real script. The decafclaw state
dir's copy points into a worktree that no longer exists.

Three things, in the order they matter:

1. The assets move into `src/agent_sessions/driver/`, beside the module that loads
   them. Verified the wheel ships them (hatch already includes non-Python files under
   the package). `driver/` now holds exactly the compatibility launcher, which is the
   coherent end state of the conversion.

2. The render fails closed. `render_hook_settings` dies on a missing, non-executable
   or unreadable asset instead of skipping. A safety control that silently omits
   itself when its asset is absent is worse than one that is missing, because nothing
   reports the difference -- that is the whole reason this survived.

3. The tests grade the code instead of the artifact. The three previous tests never
   touched the install path: one asserted a string appeared in `lifecycle.py`'s source
   text, one loaded the template by repo-relative literal and checked its shape, and
   one shelled out to `jq` to redo the substitution and asserted that jq works. They
   all passed throughout. Replaced with tests that call `preflight` and assert the
   rendered file exists, targets Bash, and names an executable that exists -- plus a
   control proving a missing template now stops the run.

`backend_permission_probe` no longer re-implements the substitution; it delegates to
`render_hook_settings`. Its own copy was the only correct resolver while the driver's
was wrong, so the probe attested to a hook no real run installed.

Also adds `git push -f` to both backends' deny lists -- the short form matched
nothing, since only `git push --force` was spelled out. Deliberately *not* adding
tool-level rules for the REST merge paths: those patterns would have to match
mid-command, `--help` does not state whether the rule syntax supports that, and an
unverified entry in a floor whose value is that it is verified is the wrong trade.
The hook covers them, now per-vector tested, and `make backend-permission-probe` is
the one live run that would settle the syntax question.

Updates the claims this move falsified: the `driver/**` allowlist clause in both
governance files now says plainly that it grants nothing, and `orientation.md`'s
layout bullets and file table point at the real locations. Its prose restatement of
the allowlist is deleted rather than corrected -- it had already drifted by omitting
`tests/**`, which is what the no-duplicate-live-sources rule exists to prevent.

Refs #261 (S1, S2, part of D3, H4).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test: stop the suites writing into the operator's home directory

There was no conftest.py anywhere in the repo, so nothing pinned XDG_STATE_HOME.
`lifecycle.preflight` derives its state dir from that variable (falling back to
$HOME/.local/state) plus `agent-session/<repo-with-dashes>`, and the fixture repo is
`owner/repo` -- so every test that drove the driver without passing --state-dir wrote
to a real path in $HOME. Measured before this change:

    ~/.local/state/agent-session/owner-repo/   897 run dirs, 1748 ledger rows, 11M
                                               plus inbox.md, parked.jsonl, workspaces/

still growing, with rows timestamped during this session's own test runs.

The worst consequence is not disk. `make evidence` reads a per-repo runs.jsonl, and
the fix for it currently reading a superseded archive is to point it at the live state
root -- at which point 1748 fabricated rows become "evidence" about runs that never
happened. So this has to land first.

An autouse fixture in the new tests/conftest.py pins the variable per test.
tests/driver/test_state_isolation.py is its control: it drives preflight with no
--state-dir and asserts the result lands inside tmp_path, plus a polarity case that
unsets the pin and confirms the fallback still resolves to the path that leaked.
Without the control this would be an assertion about the suite rather than a check on
it, which is how the original went unnoticed.

Verified: a full `make check` now leaves both counts at 897/1748, unchanged.

Second fixture, for the lock global. The full-loop harness had:

    monkeypatch.setattr(agent_session_driver, "CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE", None)
    # ... so no pass can leave a live lock behind

which did nothing -- that module binds a copy of the value at import while `locks`
mutates its own global through `global`, and nothing in src/ reads the re-exported
name. The symptom was visible on every single run: real `Releasing lock for #N...`
lines at pytest exit, the atexit hook firing after monkeypatch had restored the true
subprocess.run. Survivable only because the tmp_path repos have no `origin` to receive
a ref deletion.

Patched on the owning module, plus an autouse teardown that clears it.

Worth recording that the teardown started as an assertion that the global was already
None, and it failed at once on the full-loop passes -- correctly, because a pass that
acquires a lock and returns really does end holding it. That is the driver's designed
behaviour: the lock covers the process. Asserting against it would have been asserting
that the driver releases something it is built to keep, so the fixture resets and does
not assert. The reset is the part that removes the harm.

Refs #261 (C3, C4).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: narrow every label_manager remove list, and stop failures reading as "no labels"

`removable()` exists because `gh issue edit --remove-label X` errors when the *repo*
has no label X at all -- not just when the issue lacks it -- and a fresh target repo
only has the labels something already created, so the whole edit fails, add included.
It was applied to park, unpark and clear-attempts. `spec`, `attempt` and `merge-ready`
kept building their remove lists unconditionally.

Two of the three are on paths the driver takes on every run, and both swallow the
failure:

    parking.py:82   increment_attempts -> `attempt --count N`   except Exception: pass
    parking.py:369  apply_park_state   -> `merge-ready`         except Exception: pass

So on a fresh target repo the attempt counter silently never increments -- and the
attempt counter is the thing that stops a phase looping forever -- while the
gate-eligible success path silently fails to stamp merge-ready.

The test file's own header diagnosed this in full ("There were no tests here at all
before this file, which is why three commands carried the same bug") and then covered
only the three commands that got the fix. Eight new tests, written against the existing
FakeGh, fail with the exact production error before the change.

Second half, in scope because the first half widened its reach.
`get_current_labels` did `except Exception: return []`, making a rate limit, a 401 and a
genuinely unlabelled issue indistinguishable -- while every caller reads the result as
fact. `validate_transition` derives `is_parked` from it, so an empty list means "not
parked" and the guard permits re-speccing or re-attempting a parked issue. And now that
all six commands narrow through `removable`, an empty list would also silently skip
removals. Both are a null rendering as a positive.

It now propagates, and `main` catches it before touching anything: exit 1, a message
naming the issue, and no edit attempted. The driver's callers already wrap these in
`except Exception`, so they degrade to a no-op rather than a wrong action.

`ensure_label_exists` likewise narrowed from a bare `except RuntimeError: pass` to the
already-exists case, so a 403 from a read-only token no longer looks like success.

* refactor: give the driver's output and clock a home, breaking the barrel cycle

`agent_session_driver.py` was a 143-line re-export barrel that defined nothing, and the
package reached back through it constantly: 14 function-local imports across `lifecycle`,
`board`, `parking` and `locks`, existing purely to break the cycle the barrel created.

Two distinct things were tangled in there.

**Five spellings of one output helper set.** `say` defined four times, `log` twice, `die`
twice. Three were byte-identical; `board`'s three were trampolines that went through the
barrel to arrive at `lifecycle`'s copies. Writing one line to stdout could take three hops
through an import cycle, and which implementation you got depended on which module you
were in.

**The barrel was also the clock**, and this is the part worth stating plainly, because it
is easy to mistake for a vestige: eight call sites across five modules read
`agent_session_driver.datetime`, not because they wanted the barrel but because patching
that single attribute freezes time everywhere at once. The full-loop suite depends on it
for byte-stable `runs.jsonl` rows. That is a real and useful seam -- it was just housed in
a module whose only job was re-exporting, so every module that needed the clock had to
import the barrel from inside a function body.

New `output.py`: `say`, `log`, `die`, and `now()` as the named clock. It imports nothing
from `agent_sessions.driver`, which is what lets everything else import it at module
scope. All eight clock reads and all five output-helper definitions now route through it.

Result: function-local barrel imports drop from 14 across four modules to 7 across two --
`board.py` and `locks.py` are out of the cycle entirely. The barrel no longer re-exports
`datetime`/`timezone`, and its docstring now says what it is (an entry point that defines
nothing) and where the code actually lives, which is the single most likely thing to send
a new contributor to the wrong file.

Also removes `sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).parent))` from the barrel -- a
pre-package fossil that put the package directory itself on sys.path, making `board`,
`locks`, `gate`, `router` and `credentials` importable as bare top-level names. Nothing
needed it; every import in that file is absolute. Verified the launcher still resolves.

Two test patches had to move, and both were the same latent defect as the
CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE one fixed earlier in this branch -- patching a re-exported name:

- `test_full_loop` froze time via `setattr(agent_session_driver, "datetime", ...)`; it now
  replaces `output.now`, which is one setattr on the module that owns the clock.
- `test_driver` captured log lines via `setattr(...agent_session_driver.log, ...)`, which
  worked only because `board.log` was a call-time trampoline. It now patches `board.log`.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* refactor: import the output helpers instead of re-exporting them

Les caught this on review: `say = output.say` with a comment saying it exists
"because `agent_session_driver` and the tests import them from this module". He
asked whether that implies fixing the importers instead. It does, and the comment
was partly false.

Measured:

- **No test imports them from anywhere.** That half of the justification was
  invented. `test_driver.py` in fact documents the opposite — it patches
  `board.log` directly, with a comment explaining that patching a re-export
  "no longer reaches it, the same shape as the CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE patch that
  silently did nothing."
- **The facade did import them, from `lifecycle`**, and re-exported them in
  `__all__`, and **nothing anywhere consumed the result.** So the alias existed to
  feed a re-export that fed nobody.
- **`pr_checks.py` aliased `say` and never called it.** Purely dead.

So the chain was `output.say` -> alias in `lifecycle` -> facade imports it *from
lifecycle* -> `__all__` -> no consumer.

What it bought was a trap. A re-export of a function is a bound copy, so
`monkeypatch.setattr(agent_session_driver, "log", ...)` reads as patching the
emitter and patches nothing — which is precisely the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` defect
this branch fixes two commits earlier. Leaving `say`/`log`/`die` on the facade set
the same trap for the next person.

Now:

- `board`, `lifecycle` and `parking` bind them with a real
  `from agent_sessions.driver.output import ...`. Same brevity — `lifecycle` calls
  `say` 55 times — and `lifecycle.say` stays patchable the way the suites already
  patch `board.log`. It just no longer pretends to be a re-export.
- `pr_checks` drops the dead alias.
- The facade stops importing and exporting them, and its docstring says why.

**The clock is deliberately different.** `output.now()` stays a module-qualified
call everywhere, because a bound copy could not be frozen, and freezing it is how
the suites get deterministic timestamps. That asymmetry is now stated where it
could otherwise look like an inconsistency.

A guard pins it: nothing may put `say`/`log`/`die` back into the facade's `__all__`.
Mutation-tested — adding one back fails it. Worth asserting because the re-export is
one line and reads as harmless.

* refactor: import the output helper in locks too, and check for the rest

Les spotted `log = output.log` still in `locks.py`. It is the same remnant the
previous commit removed from five other modules, and I missed it.

`locks.py` used `output` for nothing else, so the module import goes with it.
Nothing patches `locks.log`, so there is no seam to preserve.

The reason this gets a check rather than a second tidy-up is the miss itself. The
alias and a real import bind the same object, so nothing failed and nothing could
fail — the difference is only in what the line *claims*. An assignment reads as
"this module provides `log`", which invites patching it, and patching it reaches a
copy. That is the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` trap, in the file where
`CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` lives.

One line, easy to add without thinking, invisible to every existing check, and I
grepped for it by hand and still left one. So: an AST check over the driver package
for a module-level `<name> = output.<name>`. Mutation-tested — putting the alias
back in `locks.py` fails it, naming the file and line.

`output.now()` is deliberately outside the ban and inside the check's reach. It has
to stay module-qualified so the suites can freeze the clock, and a `now = output.now`
alias is precisely what would silently break that. If one appears, this catches it.

* fix: install the merge-block hook again, and fail closed when it cannot be

The PreToolUse hook that denies `gh pr merge`, `gh api PUT .../pulls/N/merge` and the
`curl` equivalent has not been installed on any fresh state dir since the 2026-08-09
Python conversion. `lifecycle.preflight` resolved its two assets as
`Path(__file__).parent / ...` while they sat in repo-root `driver/`, so the
`if template.is_file():` guard skipped the render, nothing was written, and
`invoke_agent` went on passing `--settings <path that was never written>`.

It looked fine locally because `.driver-state/settings.json` is an Aug 6
pre-conversion leftover that happens to point at a real script. The decafclaw state
dir's copy points into a worktree that no longer exists.

Three things, in the order they matter:

1. The assets move into `src/agent_sessions/driver/`, beside the module that loads
   them. Verified the wheel ships them (hatch already includes non-Python files under
   the package). `driver/` now holds exactly the compatibility launcher, which is the
   coherent end state of the conversion.

2. The render fails closed. `render_hook_settings` dies on a missing, non-executable
   or unreadable asset instead of skipping. A safety control that silently omits
   itself when its asset is absent is worse than one that is missing, because nothing
   reports the difference -- that is the whole reason this survived.

3. The tests grade the code instead of the artifact. The three previous tests never
   touched the install path: one asserted a string appeared in `lifecycle.py`'s source
   text, one loaded the template by repo-relative literal and checked its shape, and
   one shelled out to `jq` to redo the substitution and asserted that jq works. They
   all passed throughout. Replaced with tests that call `preflight` and assert the
   rendered file exists, targets Bash, and names an executable that exists -- plus a
   control proving a missing template now stops the run.

`backend_permission_probe` no longer re-implements the substitution; it delegates to
`render_hook_settings`. Its own copy was the only correct resolver while the driver's
was wrong, so the probe attested to a hook no real run installed.

Also adds `git push -f` to both backends' deny lists -- the short form matched
nothing, since only `git push --force` was spelled out. Deliberately *not* adding
tool-level rules for the REST merge paths: those patterns would have to match
mid-command, `--help` does not state whether the rule syntax supports that, and an
unverified entry in a floor whose value is that it is verified is the wrong trade.
The hook covers them, now per-vector tested, and `make backend-permission-probe` is
the one live run that would settle the syntax question.

Updates the claims this move falsified: the `driver/**` allowlist clause in both
governance files now says plainly that it grants nothing, and `orientation.md`'s
layout bullets and file table point at the real locations. Its prose restatement of
the allowlist is deleted rather than corrected -- it had already drifted by omitting
`tests/**`, which is what the no-duplicate-live-sources rule exists to prevent.

root -- at which point 1748 fabricated rows become "evidence" about runs that never

it, which is how the original went unnoticed.

mutates its own global through `global`, and nothing in src/ reads the re-exported
name. The symptom was visible on every single run: real `Releasing lock for #N...`

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: narrow every label_manager remove list, and stop failures reading as "no labels"

`removable()` exists because `gh issue edit --remove-label X` errors when the *repo*
has no label X at all -- not just when the issue lacks it -- and a fresh target repo
only has the labels something already created, so the whole edit fails, add included.
It was applied to park, unpark and clear-attempts. `spec`, `attempt` and `merge-ready`
kept building their remove lists unconditionally.

Two of the three are on paths the driver takes on every run, and both swallow the
failure:

    parking.py:82   increment_attempts -> `attempt --count N`   except Exception: pass
    parking.py:369  apply_park_state   -> `merge-ready`         except Exception: pass

So on a fresh target repo the attempt counter silently never increments -- and the
attempt counter is the thing that stops a phase looping forever -- while the
gate-eligible success path silently fails to stamp merge-ready.

The test file's own header diagnosed this in full ("There were no tests here at all
before this file, which is why three commands carried the same bug") and then covered
only the three commands that got the fix. Eight new tests, written against the existing
FakeGh, fail with the exact production error before the change.

Second half, in scope because the first half widened its reach.
`get_current_labels` did `except Exception: return []`, making a rate limit, a 401 and a
genuinely unlabelled issue indistinguishable -- while every caller reads the result as
fact. `validate_transition` derives `is_parked` from it, so an empty list means "not
parked" and the guard permits re-speccing or re-attempting a parked issue. And now that
all six commands narrow through `removable`, an empty list would also silently skip
removals. Both are a null rendering as a positive.

It now propagates, and `main` catches it before touching anything: exit 1, a message
naming the issue, and no edit attempted. The driver's callers already wrap these in
`except Exception`, so they degrade to a no-op rather than a wrong action.

`ensure_label_exists` likewise narrowed from a bare `except RuntimeError: pass` to the
already-exists case, so a 403 from a read-only token no longer looks like success.

section describes as a dead end. Documented, along with `DRIVER_GH_BOARD_TOKEN`, and both
added to `.env.example` -- with the warning that the key belongs outside the repository,

first thing to read on a driver-fault; `parsed.json`; and `inbox.md`, which is the human
work queue every escalation appends to and had no mention in the guide at all.

rename, rather than leaving a name that shipped and then changed.

  `__all__`, and **nothing anywhere consumed the result.** So the alias existed to
  feed a re-export that fed nobody.
- **`pr_checks.py` aliased `say` and never called it.** Purely dead.

So the chain was `output.say` -> alias in `lifecycle` -> facade imports it *from
lifecycle* -> `__all__` -> no consumer.

What it bought was a trap. A re-export of a function is a bound copy, so
`monkeypatch.setattr(agent_session_driver, "log", ...)` reads as patching the
emitter and patches nothing — which is precisely the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` defect
this branch fixes two commits earlier. Leaving `say`/`log`/`die` on the facade set
the same trap for the next person.

Now:

- `board`, `lifecycle` and `parking` bind them with a real
  `from agent_sessions.driver.output import ...`. Same brevity — `lifecycle` calls
  `say` 55 times — and `lifecycle.say` stays patchable the way the suites already
  patch `board.log`. It just no longer pretends to be a re-export.
- `pr_checks` drops the dead alias.
- The facade stops importing and exporting them, and its docstring says why.

**The clock is deliberately different.** `output.now()` stays a module-qualified
call everywhere, because a bound copy could not be frozen, and freezing it is how
the suites get deterministic timestamps. That asymmetry is now stated where it
could otherwise look like an inconsistency.

A guard pins it: nothing may put `say`/`log`/`die` back into the facade's `__all__`.
Mutation-tested — adding one back fails it. Worth asserting because the re-export is
one line and reads as harmless.

* refactor: import the output helper in locks too, and check for the rest

Les spotted `log = output.log` still in `locks.py`. It is the same remnant the
previous commit removed from five other modules, and I missed it.

`locks.py` used `output` for nothing else, so the module import goes with it.
Nothing patches `locks.log`, so there is no seam to preserve.

The reason this gets a check rather than a second tidy-up is the miss itself. The
alias and a real import bind the same object, so nothing failed and nothing could
fail — the difference is only in what the line *claims*. An assignment reads as
"this module provides `log`", which invites patching it, and patching it reaches a
copy. That is the `CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` trap, in the file where
`CURRENT_LOCK_ISSUE` lives.

One line, easy to add without thinking, invisible to every existing check, and I
grepped for it by hand and still left one. So: an AST check over the driver package
for a module-level `<name> = output.<name>`. Mutation-tested — putting the alias
back in `locks.py` fails it, naming the file and line.

`output.now()` is deliberately outside the ban and inside the check's reach. It has
to stay module-qualified so the suites can freeze the clock, and a `now = output.now`
alias is precisely what would silently break that. If one appears, this catches it.

---------

Co-authored-by: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

commit.message:
fix(#261): populate the venv before make check fans out

`make check` failed on a cold .venv, deterministically:

    $ rm -rf .venv && make check
    error: Failed to install: ruff-0.16.2-py3-none-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl
    make[1]: *** [commit-lint] Error 2
    make: *** [check] Error 2

Seven jobs run under `$(MAKE) -j check-parallel` and every one of them enters
through `uv run`, which creates and populates .venv on demand. They race for it,
and one loses. Every fresh worktree hits this -- it is how the branch this lands
on was found, on its first `make check`.

What makes it worth more than a one-line fix is the shape of the failure. The
message names a wheel and an install, so it reads as a network fault or a broken
toolchain; nothing in it points at make parallelism. And the honest response --
rerun it -- succeeds, because the venv is warm by then. That trains the operator
to treat the project's only aggregate gate as flaky.

Fix: a `venv` target running `uv sync --quiet`, reached from `check`'s recipe
rather than as a prerequisite, so `make -j check` cannot reorder it.

Verified: `rm -rf .venv && make check` was exit 2 before and is exit 0 after.
The new frozen suite derives the plan from `make -n check` (which expands the
recursive sub-make) and asserts positionally that the first `uv` command sits
above the fan-out; it failed with the real diagnosis before this change. C2 is
the control -- it requires the fan-out to still be concurrent with more than one
`uv run` consumer, so C1 cannot pass by the race being refactored away silently.

New finding, not among the ones recorded on the issue.

fix(#261): make is_shim catch the facade it was written for, and name lifecycle.py

Two halves of one defect, G3 on the issue.

**The guard.** `check_partition`'s `is_shim` exists so the risk partition cannot
name a re-export facade in place of the implementation behind it -- gating a
facade reads as protection and provides none. Its predicate was a marker string,
or a 30-line ceiling on a file mentioning `from agent_sessions`. Sized for the
top-level shims #205 deleted, and wrong in both directions:

- it missed the live instance it exists for. `agent_session_driver.py` carries no
  marker and runs past 150 lines, and its own docstring opens "Defines nothing
  itself."
- it matched ordinary short modules. A file importing one helper and defining one
  function satisfied both clauses.

Length was never the property that mattered; originating nothing is. The
predicate is now an AST question -- no function and no class of its own, plus
names imported from elsewhere -- with non-Python files falling back to the marker,
since `driver/agent-session-driver.sh` is named in the partition and cannot be
parsed.

And the rule around it got more precise, not just stricter. Naming a facade is
not itself the defect: an entry point is worth gating even after it thins out,
which is exactly why the compatibility launcher is gated. The defect is a facade
standing in *for* the implementation, so the partition reads as protecting code it
never names. So the check now fails only when *none* of the modules a facade
re-exports from is named in the section. Any, not all -- the real facade
re-exports from five modules, unlisted paths are `needs-review` by default so
their absence exposes nothing, and demanding a bullet each would fill the section
with entries carrying no reason.

**The partition.** The bullet gating `agent_session_driver.py` as "the current home
of the outcome routing" was true when written and false from #256 onward, which
moved the routing to `lifecycle.classify_and_record`. The allowlist held
throughout -- unlisted `lifecycle.py` defaults to `needs-review` -- so nothing was
ever exposed. What was wrong was the stated reason, attached to a facade. Les
decided to name `lifecycle.py` explicitly; the facade keeps its own bullet with
the launcher's reason, that becoming thin does not widen the partition.

Also G2, in the same section and the same two files: the prose still placed the
detector suites at `scripts/` root level after #257/#258 moved them to
`tests/scripts/`. The Drivable bullet had been updated and the prose two
paragraphs above it had not -- the "ask what it just invalidated" shape, inside
the section that describes it.

Verified: five of the new checks failed before this change, each with the real
diagnosis, including one proving the old length heuristic was a false-positive
machine. `make docs-check` then failed on the live partition naming the facade,
naming all five modules behind it, and passes once `lifecycle.py` is named.
CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md remain byte-identical. `make check` green.

Tier: needs-review. `docs_check.py` is a gated shipping path and the partition
files are governance.

fix(#261): delete three unreachable scripts, and stop guard-lint reporting a null as a pass

**C7 -- the three scripts.** All computed the repo root as `.parent.parent`, which
after the src-layout move resolves to `src/agent_sessions`. Verified live before
deleting, rather than reasoned about:

    $ uv run python -m agent_sessions.scripts.session_artifact_stats
    Error: .../src/agent_sessions/docs/dev-sessions does not exist    exit=1
    $ uv run python -m agent_sessions.scripts.run_swarm /dev/null     exit=1

Both are broken if reached and reachable from nothing: no `[project.scripts]`
entry, no Makefile recipe, no import outside their own suites. `run_swarm` also
looks for `driver/agent_runner.py`, which the conversion deleted, so it aborts
before doing anything even with its root corrected. `validate_tdd` exists only to
serve `run_swarm`.

Les's call was to delete rather than repair -- a swarm path nothing invokes is not
worth carrying, and deleting it retires C8 (`validate_tdd` returning "compliant"
for a stream it never read) without needing a policy decision about fail-open.

`guard_lint.py` had the same wrong root, unused: `ROOT` was assigned and never
read. Deleted rather than corrected, because a constant nobody reads has no right
answer.

One reference survives and is deliberately not touched here:
`skills/agent-session/phases/execute.md:47-55` invokes `python3
scripts/run_swarm.py`, a path that predates the conversion. `skills/**` is
hard-gated, so that edit is staged separately rather than batched in.
`docs/findings.md:1032` cites `session_artifact_stats` as a runnable command and
goes with the findings.md repair.

**C10 -- guard-lint.** The recipe piped `gh issue list --json body` with no
`--limit`, so `gh` returned its default 30 newest issues and the detector printed
"no pinned test count guards found" over them. `guard_lint` had no way to know how
many records it was handed, or denied.

Measured rather than asserted: this repo has 21 open issues, so the truncation was
latent here, not active. Against `lmorchard/decafclaw` -- 141 open issues, and the
repo this detector was written for in #68 -- the old command saw 30 of 141 and
silently dropped 111.

The limit is now explicit on both sides, and a full page fails as
possibly-truncated rather than passing, which is `board_audit.bounded_records`'
rule for its reason: at the limit, truncation and coincidence are
indistinguishable. The success line now states what was examined
(`no pinned test count guards in 21 issue body(s)`), so an empty scan reads as
empty. Findings cite the real issue number instead of the array index, which used
to render as `issue #1` -- unfindable, and misleading in the direction that
matters because it looks like an issue number.

`main()` takes an explicit argv. It read `sys.argv[1:]` as file paths, so under
pytest it was linting whatever paths pytest had been given -- including, after this
commit, a test file containing pinned counts as fixtures.

**H9 -- .gitignore.** The three tool caches were ignored only because pytest, ruff
and mypy each write a nested `.gitignore` containing `*`; named explicitly now.
`.local/` added: harmless today, but the same misdirected HOME that put `gh`'s
device-id there would put its token-bearing hosts.yml there too. `runs/` is
deliberately *not* added -- `run_swarm.py` was its only producer.

Verified: four new guard-lint checks failed first, each with the real diagnosis.
`make guard-lint` reports its scope. `make check` green.

Tier: needs-review. Gated shipping paths under src/agent_sessions/scripts/.

fix(#261): make the run path call the oracle the tests exercise

C5, and it is worse than the issue records it. The issue said the divergence
"mostly still lands on no-gate ... which is why it hasn't bitten". It is
reachable, on entirely valid data, and it fails **permissive**.

**The extraction.** `gate.extract_gate` exists to find the `## Merge gate` block,
and every one of `test_gate.py`'s ~15 call sites runs
`classify(extract_gate(body))`. Production ran `classify(pr_body)` -- the whole PR
description. `gate_fields` harvests every `^key: value` line it is handed and the
first occurrence wins, and an ordinary PR summary sits *above* the gate block.

Measured, not argued:

    gate block: verdict: human-merge-required
    summary above it: "The run before this recorded  verdict: eligible-for-auto-merge"

    whole body (production)  verdict='eligible-for-auto-merge'  outcome='gate-eligible'
    extracted (tested)       verdict='human-merge-required'     outcome='gate-human'

A run whose own gate block asked for a human was classified eligible for
auto-merge, because the phrase appeared in its summary. Those two outcomes route
oppositely: one labels the PR merge-ready, the other parks the issue. A PR that
quotes a previous run's verdict while explaining what it fixed is a PR about this
harness.

Scanned 240 real PRs across both repos: 8 already classify differently under the
two paths. None flips outcome today -- they differ in harvested fields, in reason
text, and in the recorded artifact -- so this is a latent defect being closed, not
an incident being cleaned up. Worth saying plainly rather than overstating.

`gate.yaml` was affected too. `classify` returns the text it was handed, and the
driver writes that to the run directory as the run's provenance. On decafclaw #847
that is 2167 bytes of summary and design notes where a 305-byte block belongs.

**The budget rule.** `gate.budget_reclass` carries the 95% threshold and a
docstring recording why. It was referenced only from `gate.py`'s CLI and one test;
`classify_and_record` reimplemented it inline, and the copy had drifted -- no
`budget > 0` guard. With `--max-budget-usd 0` (a bare `type=float`, no lower
bound) the inline rule read `cost >= 0`, true for a run that spent nothing, so any
verdict-less outcome became `budget-exhausted`. That outcome *stops the loop*, on
the reasoning that the next issue inherits the same too-small ceiling. So a free
run under a zero ceiling halted a burndown and blamed the budget. Verified by
reverting the fix: the test fails with "stopping the loop: outcome means an
assumption is wrong".

Note this moves a threshold *into* gated `gate.py` from the coordinator. A
tightening, not a widening -- the coordinator can no longer hold its own copy.

**X4, --classify-only.** Zero coverage before this, on the branch an operator
reaches for after a run dies; `lifecycle.py` prints it as the recovery instruction
three times. Now covered: grading from the PR, recovering cost and session from a
dead run's stream, the no-PR park, and that it reaches the same oracle.

That coverage turned up a **new finding, not on the issue**:
`run_classify_only` ends by printing "recorded to runs.jsonl. Nothing was merged."
and never appends. Only `classify_and_record` opens `ctx.runs_log`. Park state *is*
applied -- so the issue is parked and the ledger this project treats as its
per-run provenance has no row for the run that parked it. The new check asserts the
discrepancy rather than either half, because which side is wrong is a decision
about the ledger's contract. Flagged for Les.

One existing assertion changed, and it is worth being explicit that this is not a
weakening: `test_pass_ending_gate_eligible` pinned `gate.yaml == the whole PR body`
with the comment "Pinned as behaviour; #184 is the fix." #184 landed the schema
validation and closed without touching the extraction, so a golden was holding the
defect in place with a pointer to an issue that had gone. It now asserts the block.
`gate_body`'s docstring carried the same stale deferral and says what happened.

Verified: both C5 checks failed through shipping `main()` before the change, the
budget check fails when reverted, `make check` green.

Tier: needs-review. `lifecycle.py` is gated, and this is the outcome routing.

fix(#261): repair the test suites' hermeticity and the Makefile's swallowed queue depth

Drivable batch: C11, H1, H3, H7, X3, and X5's fragility items.

**C11 -- the doc-rot detector's own suite cloned it instead of calling it.**
`tests/scripts/test_docs_check.py` reimplemented `check_world_state_claims` as a
local `check_line()` and asserted against the copy. `docs_check` was never
called, so the newest doc-rot rule had zero coverage through shipping code --
defect class 1 instance 9, inside the doc-rot detector's suite, and exactly the
residual risk CLAUDE.md names about leaving `tests/**` drivable.

The copy had drifted: its repo-count pattern was `\b([a-z]+) repositories\b`
against the shipped `\b(one|two|...|ten|\d+) repositories\b`, so
"Runs against many repositories" was a failure in the test and a pass in
production. It carried one exemption the shipped code lacks, omitted two it has,
and its 3-tuple predicate row kept alive a code path that is permanently dead in
the shipped 2-tuple table -- the mechanism existed only in the test.

Replaced with the real function under a patched ROOT, including a check pinning
the exact line the clone got wrong and one pinning the `file:line:` citation
format the clone discarded.

**H3 -- `make typecheck` ran `mypy src`, hiding four errors.** Three were C11,
including `"str" not callable`. The fourth was a real annotation violation in
`test_full_loop.label_ops`, whose declared `tuple[str, ...]` can be built with
`sub=None`. Fixed by asserting, not by widening: a `label_manager` call with no
subcommand would otherwise become a silent `(None, ...)` row no expected-list
would ever match on purpose. Scope is now `mypy src tests`; nothing recorded the
narrow scope as a decision, and `tests/{driver,scripts}/` came into existence
three commits before the audit, so this repairs an omission rather than reversing
a choice.

**H1 -- `make loop ISSUES=n` was swallowed.** `@$(MAKE) run ISSUES=$(or ...)`
put the assignment on the sub-make's command line, where it beats the caller's, so
`make loop ISSUES=7` ran two issues while `make help` promised otherwise -- on the
one target whose purpose is queue depth. `BUDGET ?= 35` is per issue, so a
swallowed `ISSUES=5` is a wrong-sized spend. #71, one variable over.

The obvious fix, `$(or $(ISSUES),$(LOOP_ISSUES))`, is wrong, and C2 of the new
frozen suite caught it: `ISSUES ?= 1` means `$(ISSUES)` is never empty, so `$(or)`
cannot tell "the caller asked" from "the file defaulted", and a bare `make loop`
collapsed to one issue. `$(origin)` distinguishes them. Verified across the
matrix: bare 2, `ISSUES=7` 7, `BUDGET=99` 2/99, both together 5/12, and
`ISSUES=3` from the environment 3.

The new suite covers only the slice the existing ones deliberately leave alone --
`test_run_issue_flag` cannot discover `loop` because its recipe invokes `$(MAKE)`
rather than `$(DRIVER)`, and `test_dry_run_parity` exempts `--max-issues`. The
quartet's duplication is not the bug; the uncovered slice is, and it is not
collapsed into a pattern rule.

**X3 -- 19 dead `sys.path.insert` bootstraps deleted**, made redundant by
`pythonpath = ["src"]`. The two survivors are inside `-I -S` isolated
subprocesses that test standalone importability and are correctly kept. 31 imports
left unused by the deletion, plus 14 `# noqa: E402` suppressions that only existed
because the import followed the bootstrap.

**X5 -- git config isolation.** Six suites build a throwaway repo with `git init`
and only two set an identity; everything else in the operator's global config
still applied. Reproduced rather than reasoned about: `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL` pointed
at a two-line config with `commit.gpgsign = true` breaks exactly eight tests, and
they arrive as `CalledProcessError` from a `git commit` a *fixture* ran -- so it
reads as the code under test being broken.

The first attempt was `GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null` plus `GIT_AUTHOR_*`, and the
new control test rejected it: those variables outrank *repo-level* config, so
supplying the identity that way silently re-authors the commits in the two
fixtures that set their own. A stub global config file sits below repo config in
git's precedence, which is the ordering the fixtures were written against.
Verified green under two hostile global configs (gpgsign, and hooksPath).

**X5 -- `xdist_group` was inert.** `test_gate_test_wiring.py` marks its module
because one check writes a probe test file into the tree while the other collects
it, and xdist honours the marker only under `--dist loadgroup`. `gate-test` ran
`-n auto` with no `--dist`, so the isolation was decorative, masked by the probe
file's process-unique name. Added to the recipe, with a check that asserts the
precondition rather than trusting a marker whose enabling flag lives in another
file. Group assignment is now visible in `--durations` output as `@gate_wiring`.

**X5 -- `test_discussion_manager` read the wall clock twice.** The fixture built
expected titles from `datetime.now()` and so does the module, so the two agreed
except across a UTC midnight, where it failed as a title mismatch. One frozen
instant now feeds both, patched on the module that owns the clock -- with a
control asserting the module really emits the frozen date, because without one the
freeze could be inert and the tests would pass exactly as before.

**H7 -- `park-test` misdescribed itself.** It aliased `gate-test` while `help`
promised "frozen acceptance checks for #5 (park state as a label)". Repointed at
`tests/driver/test_park_state.py` so the description is true. `driver-test` stays
an alias; CLAUDE.md cites it by name.

A stale figure worth correcting rather than repeating: X5 reports one test as
30.3s of a 35.6s run. It is now 8.86s of 11.5s. Still the single slowest, still
worth its cost, and deliberately not weakened -- it is the only thing standing
between a test file and silently never running.

Verified: every check above failed before its fix. `make check` green, and the
whole suite green under two simulated hostile git configurations.

Tier: auto-ok. Everything here is `tests/**` or `Makefile`.

fix(#261): pin CI's actions by commit, and give the workflow a permission floor

H2. `.github/workflows/check.yml` resolved three of its four steps at run time
against refs this project does not own:

    actions/checkout      uses v4   latest v7.0.1
    actions/setup-python  uses v5   latest v7.0.0
    astral-sh/setup-uv    uses v2   latest v10.0.1

A mutable tag is a tag someone else can move. CLAUDE.md gates this directory
*"because they define the environment the checks run in"* -- so the one directory
whose justification for human review is that it controls the checks was taking
`@v4` on trust, one of them eight majors stale and from a third party. That is the
loudest internal inconsistency the audit found.

SHAs resolved from each action's latest release through the API, with the version
in a trailing comment for whoever reads the diff. The comments are deliberately
*not* graded: a comment that has to agree with a SHA is a second thing to keep in
sync, and this project's documentation rule is that no doc states a fact a command
can print.

Also added, all three previously absent:

- `permissions: contents: read`. Repository settings currently default the token to
  read-only, but that is a setting and this is the repo -- a setting changes without
  a diff.
- `concurrency`, cancelling superseded PR pushes and *not* cancelling on main, so
  every commit on the default branch keeps its own result.
- `timeout-minutes: 15`. The default is six hours.

`fetch-depth: 0` kept, and now asserted: `commit-lint` scopes to
`origin/main..HEAD`, and a shallow clone does not fail the checkout -- it leaves
`commit-lint` grading an empty range and printing a pass.

`actions/setup-python` kept rather than dropped as redundant. Without it `uv`
provisions whatever interpreter satisfies `requires-python = ">=3.11"`, which is a
moving target; pinning the floor means CI grades the oldest version the project
claims to support while local development runs ahead of it. Recorded as a
deliberate choice, since nothing said so before and it read as an accident.

The new frozen suite grades the ref's *shape* rather than a list of action names --
naming the current three would rot the moment a fourth arrived, and would be a
spelling check rather than a test. Add a step and it is graded with no edit there.
Two controls, because C1 alone passes vacuously over a directory with no workflows,
and again if the discovery pattern drifts from the file's shape.

Verified: the suite fails on the pre-change workflow, naming all three unpinned
actions. `make check` green.

Not done, and flagged rather than decided: `zizmor` or `actionlint` would give this
gated directory the linter it does not have, but both are new tool dependencies and
that is a call for Les.

Tier: needs-review. `.github/**` is gated.

fix(#261): repair the instruments' stale self-citations, and stop grading YAML by substring

H10, and one defect this session introduced and then caught.

**`assertion_lint.py`'s docstring was wrong about its own detector's scope.** The
Scope section said `driver/test_*.py`; `SCOPE` is `tests/driver/test_*.py`, and
#257/#258 are what falsified the prose. A docstring wrong about the thing it
documents, inside a detector, is this repo's own recurring shape -- so the value is
no longer restated there. The paragraph points at `SCOPE` and stops.

**`commit_lint.py`'s docstring ended in an orphaned sentence fragment** --
"``assertion_lint.py`` and stay portable to a GHA runner." -- whose subject was
dropped in an edit. Reconstructed against what the module actually imports: the
standard library plus one `git log` call, no third-party dependency.

`run_progress.py`'s stale `agent-session-driver.sh:347` citation was already
repaired on the earlier branch; nothing to do.

**The presence check I wrote two commits ago, fixed.** While prototyping X1's
proposed `assert <literal> in <source_text>` rule, the one true positive it found
in the whole repo was `test_workflow_pinning.py`'s own
`assert "fetch-depth: 0" in text` -- exactly the defect class `assertion-lint`
exists for, since a comment reading *"fetch-depth: 0 was removed because..."*
satisfies it as well as the setting does. Now parsed as a key/value pair.
Verified against four inputs: the real setting yields `['0']`, a shallow clone
`['1']`, a comment mention `[]`, and prose `[]`.

X1 itself is not implemented here. Les chose "widen the scope and add the rule";
measuring both changed the picture enough that it goes back to him rather than in.
The numbers are in the next comment on #261, and `assertion_lint.py`'s Scope
section now carries them, because the reason the glob is narrow was previously
recorded only in a *sibling* detector's docstring: `commit_lint.py`'s own Scope
section says *"`assertion_lint` had to solve the same self-matching problem by
narrowing its glob."*

Tier: needs-review. Gated shipping paths under src/agent_sessions/scripts/.

fix(#261): make the recovery path record the row it says it recorded

N2, a finding X4's new coverage turned up, and Les's call on which half was wrong.

`run_classify_only` ended by printing "recorded to runs.jsonl. Nothing was
merged." Only `classify_and_record` ever opened `ctx.runs_log`. Park state *was*
applied -- so an operator recovering a dead run got the issue parked, a line
saying the ledger was written, and no row for the run that parked it. A hole in
the per-run provenance exactly where a run died, which is the case you most want
recorded, and the ledger `make evidence` and every world-state claim read.

Nothing had ever exercised `--classify-only`, which is why it survived.

Three parts:

**One row builder.** `append_run_row` is now the only place the ledger row's shape
is written, and both paths call it. The two had drifted far enough to disagree
about whether a run was recorded at all; #261's T3 names the pair as a live drift
risk, and a second hand-built copy would have re-created it on the spot.

**The inflight marker carries its phase.** `phase` is `evidence.py`'s primary
grouping key, so a recovered row without one is a run that happened and cannot be
counted -- the state the pre-#27 archive was in, and the reason every PHASE cell
used to render `unknown`. The marker is written at the start of every run and
exists to describe the run in flight, so the phase belongs in it. Markers written
before the field existed get a blank, not a crash and not a guess; that control is
asserted, because a `KeyError` here would turn the recovery path into a second
failure at the worst possible moment.

**`exit` is -1.** The run's own process never reported one, which is the situation
this path exists for. A recovered row saying `exit: 0` would be a fabrication.

Both sides of the marker coupling are asserted, in separate passes: that recovery
reads the phase, and that a normal run writes it. The producer is `invoke_agent`
and the consumer is `run_classify_only`, which is exactly the shape that goes
stale unnoticed.

The check this replaces asserted the *discrepancy* rather than either half, and
said so: "whichever way it is settled, this is the test that has to change, and
the diff will say which was chosen." It was settled in favour of recording.

Verified: all four checks failed before this change. `make check` green.

docs(#261): make AGENTS.md a pointer, and teach the parity check that shape

feat(#261): add clean, clean-venvs and prune-state, and correct H5's premise

H5 asked for three housekeeping targets. Measuring first changed what they should
do.

**The finding's premise was wrong, and acting on it would have missed the point.**
It attributes 3.2 GB to "287 run directories with no retention". Measured under
`~/.local/state/agent-session/lmorchard-decafclaw/`:

    workspaces/   3.1 GB   21 git worktrees of the target repo
    runs/          79 MB   287 per-run directories
    runs.jsonl    204 KB   the ledger

Pruning run directories reclaims 79 MB. The 3.1 GB is workspaces, and the driver
already has a mechanism for those -- `--clean-workspaces` -- that nobody passes,
which is why 21 accumulated. So both are pruned, by different rules, because they
are different things. At the default 30-day window the tool reports 1.96 GB.

**Workspaces are pruned by dirtiness, never by age**, and that is the reason this
is a script rather than a call into the existing path. `workspace.remove_workspace`
uses `git worktree remove --force`, which **does not refuse a dirty worktree**, and
`findings.md` records an incident where exactly such a worktree held the only copy
of a run's final gate block and the governance note a decision was made on. On the
live state root, **5 of 21 workspaces are dirty** -- the driver's own path would
have force-removed all five. This tool keeps them and says so. That is deliberately
the opposite default: the driver is cleaning up after a run it just supervised; an
operator running a prune is not.

An unreadable worktree counts as dirty. Defaulting the other way would make an
error look like a clean tree, which is the null-as-positive shape with data loss
as the consequence.

**Dry run is the default**, `CONFIRM=1` removes. A deletion tool whose safe mode is
the one you have to remember is the wrong way round, and printing the count means
an empty result reads as empty rather than as success.

**`runs.jsonl` is asserted unreachable, not intended to be.** Along with
`parked.jsonl`, `inbox.md` and `inflight.json`. The strong form: the checks build a
state root holding every protected file plus a stale run directory, run the tool
for real with `--confirm`, and require the protected files to survive byte for
byte. Plus a property check that every candidate is under a `runs/` directory,
since that construction -- rather than an exclusion list someone can edit past -- is
what makes the ledger safe.

`clean` deliberately leaves `.driver-state/` and the state root alone, and says so
in its own output.

One thing I got wrong twice and caught both times: backticks inside a `make` echo
are command substitution, not quoting. The second instance would have run
`make venv` as a side effect of printing help.

Tier: auto-ok. `Makefile`, `scripts/**` and `tests/**` are all drivable.

refactor(#261): give the gate's row rules one definition instead of two

T3's sharpest item, and the one that sits on the oracle.

`verify_gate_rows` and `infer_provenance` encoded the same seven row predicates
twice, line for line, differing only in what they emitted -- a verdict on one side,
a provenance record on the other. Change a rule in one and not the other and **the
gate's verdict disagrees with its own account of how it was reached**. Nothing
would have caught it: both were tested, separately, each against its own
expectations, so both suites stay green while the two disagree.

Now one `_row_failure(field, value)` says why a row fails, and both consume it.
`_row_state` layers the provenance-only distinctions on top -- `not-applicable` for
`guards: none` and a repo with no CI checks, `substituted` for a row satisfied by
something standing in for the named mechanism.

**Proved behaviour-preserving rather than asserted to be.** Before the change, the
existing implementations were replayed over a 927-case matrix -- every row varied
against a clean baseline, plus every pairwise combination of two rows, including
missing, failing, malformed and substitute-marked values. After the change the same
927 cases produce **zero differences** in either `verify_gate_rows`'s
`(ok, reasons)` or `infer_provenance`'s dict. The reason strings are byte-identical,
so a recorded run reason is unchanged.

Two subtleties the matrix pinned, both of which a naive merge would have broken:

- **`tier` has no `substituted` state.** It is a classification the skill makes, not
  evidence it gathers, so there is nothing for a substitute to stand in for. Every
  other row has the state; a shared code path has to keep the exception.
- **Failure outranks substitution.** `threads: 1 unresolved -- via substitute` is
  `failed`, not `substituted`. The interesting thing about a wrong answer is not how
  it was arrived at.

**And the coupling is now asserted.** Seven parametrised checks require that a row
which fails the verdict also reads `failed` in provenance, with a control requiring
a clean block to do neither. Mutation-tested: re-inlining one row's rule into
`infer_provenance` alone -- the exact drift this removes -- fails two of them.

`"failing" in ci.upper()`, which can never be true, since `.upper()` produces no
lowercase. `"fail" in ci.lower()` already covered it, which is why nothing noticed.

X2, in the form the defect actually takes.

`test_workspace_driver_integration.py` monkeypatched `subprocess.run` with a
catch-all:

    class MockResult:
        stdout = "{}"
        returncode = 0
    ...
    return MockResult()     # everything not specifically matched

`test_full_loop.py`'s docstring names this exact anti-pattern as the reason
`FakeGitHub.unhandled` exists. The consequence is that all three tests **would have

and the test would silently grade a fallback branch.

makes is now modelled by shape. Re-run of the same mutation with a call the driver
has never made fails all three tests.

  `tests/conftest.py` instead, and `pyproject.toml` is untouched.
- **Moving `FakeGitHub`, `StubAgent` and `LoopHarness` into a shared conftest**, the
  other half of X2. Deliberately not done: a ~700-line mechanical move of a working
  harness, whose payoff is reuse rather than correctness, and the defect X2 is about
  is the silent success -- which this closes without it. Left as a clean follow-up.

The catch-all sites in `test_driver.py` are also untouched. They are narrow unit
tests whose stubs answer one or two specific shapes, and converting them buys much
less than converting the three integration passes did.

Tier: auto-ok. `tests/**` only.

Session artifacts were 326 of 443 tracked files, 203 of them microtest result JSON
from a single 2026-07-27 study, which dominated every `git ls-files` and grep a

them rather than delete them.

caught in the script itself, both worth naming since they are the reason it is a
script:

- The rewrite was not idempotent. `dev-sessions/X` is a substring of its own
  corrected form `archive/dev-sessions/X`, so re-running yielded

  applied run is now safe to re-drive -- which mattered, because the first run
  died between its move pass and its rewrite pass.

  broke on the extra nesting level, and two of the nine *shorten* rather than
  lengthen, so adjusting `../` counts by arithmetic would have been wrong. It now
  resolves each link against the old directory and re-derives it from the new one.

- `testpaths = ["driver", "scripts"]` pointed at directories that now hold only

  a file. Removed; lint passes without them, which confirms they were vestigial

test files can be deleted, and extends ruff's exclude to `docs/archive` to match

exclude and into the linter -- which broke `make lint` on the previous commit.
