issue.body:
<!-- agent-session:spec -->

## Context

The instrumentation added in #623 (#310, #409) writes append-only JSONL sidecars under `workspace/`:

- `workspace/tool_usage.jsonl` — one record per tool call
- `workspace/reflection/metrics.jsonl` — one record per judge-eligible turn

These have **no rotation or retention** — they grow unbounded. This was an explicit, documented deferral in the instrumentation session ("append-only; retention is a follow-up"), acceptable for the initial ~week-of-data measurement window but not indefinitely.

The Copilot review on #623 already prompted a mitigation: `load_records()` in both `tool_telemetry.py` and `reflection_metrics.py` now streams the file line-by-line instead of reading it whole, so the reports tolerate growth better in the meantime. But the files still accumulate forever.

## Options to weigh

- **Time-based retention** — drop records older than N days on write or via a periodic sweep (mirrors `notifications.retention_days`, which is the closest existing precedent).
- **Size/line-based rotation** — cap at N lines, trimming oldest on append (mirrors `notes.max_total_entries`).
- **On-demand SQLite index** — the #310 spec floated this for long-window query ergonomics; probably premature until the report CLIs feel slow.

Retention config would naturally live on `TelemetryConfig` (e.g. `retention_days` and/or `max_entries`), defaulting to something generous.

## Decide with data first

Worth checking real file growth after a few weeks of the default-on telemetry running before picking a mechanism — the right cap depends on actual per-day volume.

## Related
- #623 (instrumentation PR), #310, #409
- Precedent: `NotificationsConfig.retention_days`, `NotesConfig.max_total_entries`

---

<!-- Appended by agent-session:triage & refined on 2026-08-14 following human decision (Option a). -->

## Human Decision

- **Selected Option:** (a) Notifications-style archive — move old records to monthly archives (zero data loss).
- **Scope:** Includes `tool_usage.jsonl`, `reflection/metrics.jsonl`, and `telemetry/retrieval.jsonl`.

## Verifiable Acceptance Criteria

- CRITERION: `TelemetryConfig` SHALL define `retention_days: int = 30`.
  CHECK: `uv run python -c "from decafclaw.config_types import TelemetryConfig; assert hasattr(TelemetryConfig(), 'retention_days'); assert TelemetryConfig().retention_days == 30"` passes.

- CRITERION: Telemetry writing for `tool_usage.jsonl`, `reflection/metrics.jsonl`, and `telemetry/retrieval.jsonl` SHALL opportunistically rotate records older than `retention_days` into monthly archive files under an archive directory (mirroring notifications rotation), keeping recent records in the primary log.
  CHECK: `uv run pytest tests/test_telemetry_rotation.py` passes.

## Regression Guards

- GUARD: `uv run pytest tests/test_tool_telemetry.py tests/test_reflection_metrics.py tests/test_retrieval_telemetry.py -q` passes.
- GUARD: Fail-open write safety is preserved across rotation.

## Tier: auto-ok

commit.message:
fix: restore web client — remove import of never-emitted TS api-client

`static/` is served verbatim by StaticFiles and nothing transpiles app
code, so `auth-client.js:1` importing './api-client/index.js' 404'd: only
`index.ts` was ever emitted (`tsconfig.json` is noEmit). `app.js` imports
auth-client on its 7th line, so the browser aborted the entry module's
subgraph and the whole web UI failed to boot.

`make check` could not catch it. `moduleResolution: "bundler"` makes tsc
rewrite the specifier './api-client/index.js' to index.ts and call it
valid — the typechecker was modelling a build step that does not exist.

Revert `checkSession` to the `fetch` its own siblings still use (`login`
and `logout` were never migrated), byte-identical to the pre-#825 blob.

Also drop the zero-byte `lib/api-client.ts` and the Makefile `touch` that
fabricated it. It existed only to satisfy `test_api_codegen.py`, which
asserted that path while the codegen tool emits a directory tree — the
test passed by checking an artifact the build created for it. Retarget it
at the real output, and delete the always-green `pass`-body stub whose
stated intent ("schema change breaks frontend") is now actually covered.

Guards added, both verified to fail when the import is reintroduced:
- `test_web_static_module_graph.py` — every specifier in a browser-served
  module resolves on disk (walks 51 modules from app.js)
- `test_api_codegen.py` — served code does not import the generated client

Generated client left in place but unimported; #843 tracks the real work,
since every route signature is currently param-less returning `any`.

Note: `make check-js` fails on an unrelated pre-existing lit `css`
interpolation error in `widgets/json_view/widget.js:26`, identically on
pristine origin/main. Untouched here.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

test: close two holes in the new static-module guards

Both from Copilot review on #844, both verified against the tree before
changing anything.

`_resolve` accepted a specifier that climbs out of the mount. `..` does
not mean the same thing on both sides: the browser clamps at the URL root,
so `../../../foo.js` from `/static/lib/` requests `/foo.js` — off the mount,
always a 404 — while `pathlib` keeps walking up into the repo and can land
on a real file. Verified: an escaping import pointing at a file that exists
outside `static/` passed before, fails now with the reason named.

The api-client guard scanned `*.test.js`, which its own docstring excludes
from "browser-served". Those files are never served and vitest transpiles
TS, so a unit test importing the client is legitimate. Now excluded, as in
the sibling test.

Also tightened that guard's detection while in there: it matched
`api-client/` anywhere in the file, so a comment mentioning the path
counted as a reference. Now requires `from` / `import` context. Verified
all three ways — a `*.test.js` import and a comment mention no longer trip
it, a real import in served code still does.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: json_view widget threw at module load, breaking make check-js

`make check-js` has been red on main independent of this PR:

  widgets/json_view/widget.js(26,21): error TS2345: Argument of type
  'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number | CSSResultGroup'

Not cosmetic. lit's `css` tag *throws* on any interpolation that is not a
number or CSSResult, and `static styles` is a static class field evaluated
at class-definition time — so `max-height: ${INLINE_MAX_HEIGHT}` with a
plain-string constant threw the moment the module was imported. The widget
could never load. Verified against the vendored lit:

  Value passed to 'css' function must be a 'css' function result: 20rem.

The constant had exactly one use. `unsafeCSS()` would also work, but it
imports lit's escape hatch to inject a hardcoded literal and invites the
next person to reach for it with a value that genuinely isn't safe — so
inline the literal and drop the constant.

Verified in a real browser (static-only harness using the app's own import
map, no bot instance): module imports cleanly, exports JsonViewWidget, its
styles.cssText contains `max-height: 20rem`, and it renders a JSON tree.
`make check-js` now exits 0 for the first time.

Note this is *why* the error survived: a red gate emits no signal, so new
breakage hides behind existing breakage. Green restores tsc's ability to
catch the next TS2345 — which is the guard for this class, so no new test.

Unrelated observation, left alone: json_view is the only widget using
shadow DOM + a `css` template; the other ten use
`createRenderRoot() { return this; }` for light DOM. Converting it would
change CSS inheritance and wants its own visual check.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

issue.title: fix: restore web client — remove import of never-emitted TS api-client
issue.body:
## Symptom

`GET /static/lib/api-client/index.js` → **404**, and the entire web UI fails to boot.

## Root cause

PR #825 generated a TypeScript OpenAPI client into `static/` and pointed `auth-client.js` at it:

```js
// static/lib/auth-client.js:1
import { DefaultService } from './api-client/index.js';
```

Only `index.ts` was ever emitted. `static/` is served verbatim (`http_server.py:2487`), `make vendor` bundles only third-party deps, and `tsconfig.json` is `"noEmit": true` — so nothing ever produced `index.js`.

`app.js:7` imports `auth-client.js`, and a 404 on any ES-module specifier aborts the **whole subgraph**. One missing leaf → the entry module never evaluates → blank UI.

Reproduced against the real mount:

```
200 /static/app.js
200 /static/lib/auth-client.js
404 /static/lib/api-client/index.js   ← the break
200 /static/lib/api-client/index.ts
```

### Why `make check` stayed green for three days

`moduleResolution: "bundler"` makes tsc rewrite the specifier `./api-client/index.js` to `index.ts` and call it valid. **The typechecker was modelling a build step that does not exist.** Compounding it: `tsconfig.json`'s `include` is `["app.js", "lib/**/*.js", …]`, so the `.ts` files weren't even in scope, and no test loads the module graph.

## Fix

Revert `checkSession` to the `fetch` its own siblings still use — `login()` and `logout()` in that same file were never migrated, so the file was already inconsistent. The result is **byte-identical to the pre-#825 blob**.

## Cleanup

`lib/api-client.ts` was a zero-byte file the Makefile `touch`ed into place solely to satisfy `test_api_codegen.py`, which asserted that path even though the codegen tool emits a *directory tree*. The test passed by checking an artifact the build fabricated for it. Removed both; retargeted the test at the real output. Also deleted `test_c2_schema_change_breaks_frontend`, an always-green `pass`-body stub whose stated intent is now genuinely covered.

## Guards

Both **verified to fail** when the import is reintroduced, then pass when reverted:

- **`tests/test_web_static_module_graph.py`** — every import specifier in a browser-served module must resolve on disk. Catches this whole bug class, not just this file. Skips bare specifiers (import map) and `*.test.js` (never served; vitest resolves `?raw` and JSON imports the browser can't).
- **`tests/test_api_codegen.py`** — served code must not import the generated client, with the reason attached.

Supplementary: walked the real graph over HTTP from `app.js` — **51 modules, zero failures**.

## What's deliberately left

The generated client stays in place but unimported. #843 tracks the real work: every route signature is currently param-less returning `any` (`wrapperApiConversationsIdGet()` has no way to pass the `{id}`), because the routes are untyped `wrapper` functions. Adding an emit step first would ship a build dependency for a client with zero type safety — **type the routes first**.

## Verification

| Gate | Result |
|---|---|
| `pytest tests/ contrib/skills/` | **3870 passed**, 2 skipped |
| `vitest run` | **178 passed** (20 files) |
| `ruff check src/ tests/` | clean |
| `pyright` | 0 errors, 0 warnings |
| module graph over HTTP | 51 modules, 0 failures |
| `make check-js` | **exit 0** (was red on main) |

### `make check-js` — was pre-existing, now fixed here (scope added mid-review)

Added the `make check-js` fix here per request (643336c). It turned out to be more than a type complaint.

## It was a real runtime bug

```
widgets/json_view/widget.js(26,21): error TS2345: Argument of type 'string'
is not assignable to parameter of type 'number | CSSResultGroup'
```

lit's `css` tag **throws** on any interpolation that isn't a number or `CSSResult`, and `static styles` is a static class field — evaluated at *class-definition* time, i.e. module load. So `max-height: ${INLINE_MAX_HEIGHT}` with a plain-string constant threw the instant anything imported the module. **The `json_view` widget could never load.** Confirmed against the vendored lit:

```
Value passed to 'css' function must be a 'css' function result: 20rem.
```

## Fix

The constant had exactly one use. `unsafeCSS()` would also work, but it pulls in lit's escape hatch to inject a hardcoded literal and invites the next person to reach for it with a value that genuinely isn't safe — so I inlined the literal and dropped the constant.

## Verified in a real browser

Static-only harness using the app's own import map (no bot instance started):

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| module imports | clean, exports `JsonViewWidget` |
| `styles.cssText` | contains `max-height: 20rem` |
| renders | real JSON tree — `$: { 2 items alpha: 1 … }` |
| `make check-js` | **exit 0** — green for the first time |

Full gates: 3870 pytest · 178 vitest · ruff clean · pyright 0 errors.

## Why it survived this long

A red gate emits no signal — new breakage hides behind existing breakage. Making it green is what restores tsc's ability to catch the next TS2345, which is the guard for this class, so I didn't add a test for it.

## Left alone deliberately

`json_view` is the only widget using shadow DOM + a `css` template; the other ten use `createRenderRoot() { return this; }` for light DOM (`diff_view` comments *"Use light DOM to inherit CSS"*, `terminal` says *"matches other widgets"*). +and pointed `auth-client.js` at `./api-client/index.js`, but only

+rewrite the specifier `./api-client/index.js` to `index.ts` and call it
+valid — the typechecker was modelling a build step that does not exist.
+
+Test files are excluded: they are never served, and vitest resolves things
+the browser cannot (`?raw` suffixes, bare JSON imports).
+"""
+
+import pathlib
+import re
+
+STATIC_DIR = (
+    pathlib.Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
+    / "src"
+    / "decafclaw"
+    / "web"
+    / "static"
+)
+

+# is esbuild output (`make vendor`) and `node_modules/` is npm's.
+EXCLUDED_DIRS = {"node_modules", "vendor"}
+

+# single- and double-quoted literals — a template literal is not statically
+# resolvable, so there is nothing to check.
+_SPECIFIER_RE = re.compile(
+    r"""(?:\bfrom\s*|\bimport\s*\(?\s*)['"]([^'"]+)['"]"""
+)
+
+
+def _served_modules() -> list[pathlib.Path]:
+    return [
+        path
+        for path in sorted(STATIC_DIR.rglob("*.js"))
+        if not EXCLUDED_DIRS & set(path.relative_to(STATIC_DIR).parts)
+        and not path.name.endswith(".test.js")
+    ]
+
+
+def _specifiers(path: pathlib.Path) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
+    found = []
+    for lineno, line in enumerate(path.read_text().splitlines(), start=1):
+        for match in _SPECIFIER_RE.finditer(line):
+            found.append((lineno, match.group(1)))

+
+def _resolve(source: pathlib.Path, specifier: str) -> pathlib.Path | None:
+    """Where the browser would look, or None if it wouldn't look on disk.
+
+    Bare specifiers (`lit`, `@milkdown/kit`) go through the import map in

issue.body:
Follow-up to #785 / PR #825. Split out of the hotfix in #844, which unbroke the web UI by removing the only importer of the generated client.

## What's wrong

PR #825 added a generated TypeScript client at `src/decafclaw/web/static/lib/api-client/` and pointed `auth-client.js` at `./api-client/index.js`. Two independent problems:

**1. Nothing emits `.js`.** `static/` is served verbatim by `StaticFiles` (`http_server.py:2487`) and `tsconfig.json` is `"noEmit": true` — `make check-js` type-checks but never builds. So `index.js` never existed and the import 404'd, which aborted the `app.js` module subgraph and blanked the entire web UI for three days.

`make check` could not catch it: `moduleResolution: "bundler"` makes tsc rewrite the specifier `./api-client/index.js` to `index.ts` and call it valid. The typechecker was modelling a build step that doesn't exist. `tests/test_web_static_module_graph.py` now guards this class of bug structurally.

**2. The generated signatures carry no type information.** The routes are registered as untyped `wrapper` functions, so codegen produced 60+ methods that take **no parameters** and return `CancelablePromise<any>`:

\`\`\`ts
public static wrapperApiConversationsIdGet(): CancelablePromise<any> {
    return __request(OpenAPI, { method: 'GET', url: '/api/conversations/{id}' });
}
\`\`\`

There is no way to pass the `{id}`. Only `authMeApiAuthMeGet()` has a real return type (`UserResponse`), because `/api/auth/me` is the one route with a Pydantic response model.

## Why order matters

Adding an emit step alone would ship a build dependency for a client that still provides zero type safety — the stated goal of #785. **Type the routes first**, then wire up emit.

## Work

- [ ] Give routes real FastAPI signatures (path/query params, Pydantic request + response models) so codegen produces usable types. Incremental: one route group at a time.
- [ ] Decide the emit strategy — `tsc` emit for `lib/api-client/` only, or fold it into the existing esbuild setup (`make vendor` / `build-vendor.mjs`).
- [ ] Wire generation + emit into `make check` so a stale or unbuilt client fails CI rather than 404ing in the browser.
- [ ] Migrate frontend callers off hand-rolled `fetch`.

Until then `api-client/` is generated-but-unimported, and `make gen-api-client` / `scripts/gen_api_client.py` carry comments saying so.

issue.body:
## Context

`shell_tools.py`'s `check_shell_approval()` asks the user about every dangerous-looking command. Hermes-agent's `approval.py` adds a smart pre-approval: an aux LLM screens proposed commands and auto-approves trivially-safe ones (`ls`, `git status`, `cat`, `python -V`) without nagging the user.

Pairs naturally with the auxiliary LLM client (#452).

## Proposed approach

- Extend `check_shell_approval()`:
  1. Existing pattern allowlist → instant approve.
  2. Existing pattern denylist → instant deny / always-confirm.
  3. **New**: aux LLM call with command + cwd; returns `{auto_approve: bool, reason: str, risk: low|medium|high}`.
  4. `auto_approve: true` → proceed; log the decision + reason for audit.
  5. `auto_approve: false` → fall through to existing user confirmation.
- Per-session memory of LLM-approved patterns so repeated `ls -la` doesn't re-call the aux LLM each time.
- Config: `shell.aux_approval_enabled` (default `false` until trusted).

## Validation

- Test: aux LLM returns approve, no user confirmation triggered.
- Test: aux LLM returns deny, falls through to user confirmation.
- Test: aux LLM unavailable / errors out → fail-closed (user confirmation as today).
- Audit: every aux-LLM decision logged with command + risk + reason.

## Open questions

- This is sensitive — wrong-side errors mean the agent runs commands the user wouldn't have approved. Worth a brainstorm before enabling by default.
- Should "low risk" auto-approve while "medium risk" still confirm but with a pre-filled "looks safe because X" hint?

## Depends on

#452 (auxiliary LLM client).

## Reference

`hermes-agent/tools/approval.py`.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN `check_shell_approval()` evaluates a command matching an existing allowlist pattern THE SYSTEM SHALL immediately approve it without calling the auxiliary LLM.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_allowlist_bypasses_aux_llm` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails or missing today before implementation.

- CRITERION: WHEN `check_shell_approval()` evaluates a command not on the allowlist or denylist THE SYSTEM SHALL invoke the auxiliary LLM with command and cwd, and WHEN the auxiliary LLM returns `auto_approve: true` THE SYSTEM SHALL approve the command and log the decision and reason.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_aux_llm_auto_approve` (using mock aux LLM client) passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today (aux approval logic not yet implemented).

- CRITERION: WHEN the auxiliary LLM returns `auto_approve: false` or errors out / is unavailable THE SYSTEM SHALL fall through to user confirmation (fail-closed).
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_aux_llm_deny_or_error_falls_through` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today.

## Regression guards

- GUARD: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py` — existing shell approval tests stay green. Passes today.

## Tier: auto-ok

**Reason:** All criteria are verifiable with unit tests against mock aux LLM clients, dependency #452 is closed, and default risk threshold behavior (only `auto_approve: true` auto-approves, everything else falls through to user confirmation) is approved by the user.

## Design decisions

- **Decision:** Only `auto_approve: true` (low risk / explicitly approved by aux LLM) auto-approves; everything else falls through to user confirmation.
  - **Why:** Approved by user in issue discussion; maintains fail-closed safety for medium/high risk or uncertain responses.
- **Decision:** Dependency #452 (auxiliary LLM client) is closed and available.
  - **Why:** Unlocks aux LLM integration for command screening.

commit.message:
feat(driver): check REST core rate limit and check rate limit per issue candidate (#242)

* fix(reconciler): ignore STALE_CHANGES_REQUESTED to avoid duplicate address_comments passes

When a PR receives a CHANGES_REQUESTED review, the driver correctly enters the
address_comments phase and pushes new commits. However, because GitHub
preserves the CHANGES_REQUESTED state on the PR unless the repo is explicitly
configured to dismiss stale reviews, the driver would repeatedly see
reviewDecision == CHANGES_REQUESTED and trigger address_comments again in an
infinite loop (until max attempts are reached).

By adding the 'commits' field to the gh pr list JSON and comparing the latest
commit's date with the latest CHANGES_REQUESTED review's date, we detect when
the agent has already pushed code addressing the review. This causes the
reconciler to correctly fall through to grade_gate and park the PR for human
review.

* feat(driver): check REST core rate limit and check rate limit per issue candidate

issue.body:
## Context

The agent workspace tends to accumulate clutter — loose files in the root, half-finished drafts, stale `tmp/` artifacts, ad-hoc naming. There is no conventional structure beyond a couple of reserved subdirectories (`skills/`, `conversations/`, `tmp/`, `todos/`, the vault). Two gaps contribute:

1. **Tool gap** — the agent can not cleanly manage directories. `workspace_write` creates a file (and its parent dirs as a side effect), but there is no dedicated way to create an empty directory, remove a non-empty one, or copy a file. `workspace_move` and `workspace_delete` are file-oriented and may not handle directories well. The agent falls back to `shell` for these, which needs confirmation each time.

2. **Guidance gap** — AGENT.md does not suggest how to organize working files. The agent dumps output into the root without a project or topic structure, then has trouble finding things later.

## Proposal

### A. New / extended tools

- **`workspace_mkdir(path)`** — create an empty directory (and parents). No-op if it exists. Needed for scaffolding project layouts up front.
- **`workspace_copy(src, dest)`** — copy a file within the workspace. Useful for templating ("start from this draft") and checkpoints.
- **Extend `workspace_delete`** to handle directories: require a `recursive: true` flag for non-empty dirs; refuse otherwise. Empty dirs delete freely.
- **Extend `workspace_move`** to handle directories if it does not already.
- **Consider `workspace_exists(path)`** — a cheap existence check that does not error. Minor; could fold into `workspace_list` or `workspace_read` semantics.

Each should respect the existing sandbox boundary (`_resolve_safe`) and return `ToolResult` with useful status text.

### B. Organizational guidance

Add a short "Workspace organization" section to AGENT.md (or a dedicated `organize` skill if it needs to grow) suggesting a default structure:

- `tmp/` — scratch space for the current turn or a very short series. Files here can be deleted freely at any time.
- `projects/<name>/` — working files grouped by project or topic. When you start a multi-file effort, mkdir a folder for it rather than dropping files in the root.
- `drafts/` — in-progress writing (blog posts, docs) before they land in the vault or an external repo.
- Do not leave the workspace root cluttered — periodically sweep or organize.

Framing it as guidance rather than a hard structure. Different workflows may justify different layouts; the agent should suggest organization rather than rigidly enforce it.

### C. Optional: cleanup sweep

A bundled skill or scheduled task that periodically:
- Lists stale files in `tmp/` (e.g., older than N days) and offers to delete them
- Flags files at the workspace root that look like they should be filed elsewhere

This is a nice-to-have and could come later.

## Scope note

Pieces A and B are the core value and could ship in one PR. Piece C is speculative. A benefits from B — adding `workspace_mkdir` is low value without guidance that encourages the agent to actually *use* directory structure.

## Related

- #17 / project skill — precedent for bundled structured workflows
- Existing `workspace_*` tools in `src/decafclaw/tools/workspace_tools.py`
- Vault already has a conventional structure (`agent/pages`, `agent/journal`) that the workspace lacks

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN `workspace_mkdir` is invoked with a relative path, THE SYSTEM SHALL create the directory and all parent directories successfully and return a success message.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_workspace_tools.py::test_workspace_mkdir` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today because `workspace_mkdir` does not exist.

- CRITERION: WHEN `workspace_copy` is invoked with a valid source file and destination path, THE SYSTEM SHALL copy the file content to the destination and return success.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_workspace_tools.py::test_workspace_copy` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today because `workspace_copy` does not exist.

- CRITERION: WHEN `workspace_delete` is invoked on a directory with `recursive: true`, THE SYSTEM SHALL delete the directory and its contents recursively and return success; AND WHEN invoked on a non-empty directory without `recursive: true`, THE SYSTEM SHALL return an error indicating it is a directory and suggesting shell use.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_workspace_tools.py::test_workspace_delete_directory` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today because `workspace_delete` rejects directories.

## Tier: auto-ok

All criteria are unit-testable against workspace tools and do not touch risk-gated paths (auth, credentials, core config, database migrations).

commit.message:
fix(reconciler): ignore STALE_CHANGES_REQUESTED to avoid duplicate address_comments passes (#241)

When a PR receives a CHANGES_REQUESTED review, the driver correctly enters the
address_comments phase and pushes new commits. However, because GitHub
preserves the CHANGES_REQUESTED state on the PR unless the repo is explicitly
configured to dismiss stale reviews, the driver would repeatedly see
reviewDecision == CHANGES_REQUESTED and trigger address_comments again in an
infinite loop (until max attempts are reached).

By adding the 'commits' field to the gh pr list JSON and comparing the latest
commit's date with the latest CHANGES_REQUESTED review's date, we detect when
the agent has already pushed code addressing the review. This causes the
reconciler to correctly fall through to grade_gate and park the PR for human
review.

issue.body:
**Concept from opencode:**
Agent frameworks are difficult to debug. `opencode` embeds **OpenTelemetry (OTLP)** natively. Tool calls, LLM requests, and database transactions emit distributed trace spans, allowing developers to visualize waterfall execution graphs in tools like Jaeger or Honeycomb.

**How `decafclaw` could implement this:**
`decafclaw` uses a homegrown telemetry solution (subscribing to `EventBus` for `tool_telemetry` and `reflection_metrics`) and relies on `LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG`, which is noisy and hard to analyze for performance bottlenecks.

**Proposed Implementation:**
- Integrate `opentelemetry-api` and `opentelemetry-sdk` into the Python backend.
- Instrument critical pathways (e.g., `ContextComposer.compose`, `execute_single_tool`, `TurnRunner._run_iteration`, and the LLM client) with `@tracer.start_as_current_span()`.
- Provide an optional OTLP exporter configuration so users/developers can easily spin up a local Jaeger container to visually debug slow agent turns or loop-breaker triggers.

### Design decisions
- **Decision:** Proceed with adding OpenTelemetry dependencies (`opentelemetry-api` and `opentelemetry-sdk`).
- **Why:** The proposed implementation relies on these dependencies. The human reviewer explicitly approved adding them in the ratification pass.

### Acceptance Criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN an OTLP exporter is configured, the system SHALL start an OpenTelemetry trace span for each agent turn, tool execution, and context composition.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_telemetry_otlp.py::test_otlp_spans_started_on_core_pathways` passes (asserts using a `MemorySpanExporter` that spans are created for `run_iteration`, `execute_single_tool`, and `ContextComposer.compose`).

- CRITERION: WHEN an OTLP exporter is configured, the LLM client SHALL emit OTLP spans for its requests.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_telemetry_otlp.py::test_llm_client_emits_span` passes (asserts span creation wrapping the LLM provider call).

- CRITERION: WHEN an OTLP exporter is NOT configured, the system SHALL use a NoOp tracer and SHALL NOT attempt to export spans.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_telemetry_otlp.py::test_no_otlp_exporter_configured` passes.

### Regression Guards

- GUARD: The existing homegrown telemetry (e.g., `tool_telemetry`, `reflection_metrics`) over `EventBus` SHALL continue to function without modification.
  CHECK: The existing test suite (`make test`) stays green, meaning no `tool_telemetry` or `EventBus` tests fail or are newly skipped.

## Tier: auto-ok
**Reason:** The human reviewer (lmorchard) explicitly approved adding `opentelemetry-api` and `opentelemetry-sdk` dependencies in the issue comments. All acceptance criteria have runnable `pytest` checks.

issue.title: Telemetry log rotation/retention (tool_usage.jsonl, reflection/metrics.jsonl)

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: agent-session:needs-human
labels.description: the agent-session driver parked this issue

labels.name: agent-session:auto-ok
labels.description: Verifiable criteria satisfied and ready for autonomous execution

issue.body:
<!-- agent-session:spec -->

## Context

The instrumentation added in #623 (#310, #409) writes append-only JSONL sidecars under `workspace/`:

- `workspace/tool_usage.jsonl` — one record per tool call
- `workspace/reflection/metrics.jsonl` — one record per judge-eligible turn

These have **no rotation or retention** — they grow unbounded. This was an explicit, documented deferral in the instrumentation session ("append-only; retention is a follow-up"), acceptable for the initial ~week-of-data measurement window but not indefinitely.

The Copilot review on #623 already prompted a mitigation: `load_records()` in both `tool_telemetry.py` and `reflection_metrics.py` now streams the file line-by-line instead of reading it whole, so the reports tolerate growth better in the meantime. But the files still accumulate forever.

## Options to weigh

- **Time-based retention** — drop records older than N days on write or via a periodic sweep (mirrors `notifications.retention_days`, which is the closest existing precedent).
- **Size/line-based rotation** — cap at N lines, trimming oldest on append (mirrors `notes.max_total_entries`).
- **On-demand SQLite index** — the #310 spec floated this for long-window query ergonomics; probably premature until the report CLIs feel slow.

Retention config would naturally live on `TelemetryConfig` (e.g. `retention_days` and/or `max_entries`), defaulting to something generous.

## Decide with data first

Worth checking real file growth after a few weeks of the default-on telemetry running before picking a mechanism — the right cap depends on actual per-day volume.

## Related
- #623 (instrumentation PR), #310, #409
- Precedent: `NotificationsConfig.retention_days`, `NotesConfig.max_total_entries`

---

<!-- Appended by agent-session:triage & refined on 2026-08-14 following human decision (Option a). -->

## Human Decision

- **Selected Option:** (a) Notifications-style archive — move old records to monthly archives (zero data loss).
- **Scope:** Includes `tool_usage.jsonl`, `reflection/metrics.jsonl`, and `telemetry/retrieval.jsonl`.

## Verifiable Acceptance Criteria

- CRITERION: `TelemetryConfig` SHALL define `retention_days: int = 30`.
  CHECK: `uv run python -c "from decafclaw.config_types import TelemetryConfig; assert hasattr(TelemetryConfig(), 'retention_days'); assert TelemetryConfig().retention_days == 30"` passes.

- CRITERION: Telemetry writing for `tool_usage.jsonl`, `reflection/metrics.jsonl`, and `telemetry/retrieval.jsonl` SHALL opportunistically rotate records older than `retention_days` into monthly archive files under an archive directory (mirroring notifications rotation), keeping recent records in the primary log.
  CHECK: `uv run pytest tests/test_telemetry_rotation.py` passes.

## Regression Guards

- GUARD: `uv run pytest tests/test_tool_telemetry.py tests/test_reflection_metrics.py tests/test_retrieval_telemetry.py -q` passes.
- GUARD: Fail-open write safety is preserved across rotation.

## Tier: auto-ok

issue.body:
Event bus subscriber for metrics: response times, tool usage, error rates, circuit breaker trips.

**What to track:**
- LLM call latency (per model)
- Tool call frequency and duration
- Error rates by tool
- Compaction frequency and duration
- MCP server health (connected/failed/reconnects)
- Heartbeat cycle duration
- Conversation count and message volume

**Output options:**
- Structured log lines (JSON) that can be parsed by log aggregators
- Prometheus metrics endpoint (pairs with health check endpoint #12)
- SQLite metrics table for simple querying
- Event bus makes this easy — just subscribe and record

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN an LLM call completes, THE SYSTEM SHALL record its latency per model and make it queryable via the metrics subsystem or SQLite table.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_metrics.py::test_llm_call_latency_recorded` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails currently because `test_metrics.py` or the latency tracking does not exist yet.

- CRITERION: WHEN a tool call executes, THE SYSTEM SHALL record its frequency, duration, and error status by tool name.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_metrics.py::test_tool_usage_metrics_recorded` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails currently because tool usage metrics recording is not implemented.

- CRITERION: WHEN the metrics or health endpoints are requested, THE SYSTEM SHALL expose structured metrics (JSON / Prometheus / SQLite table).
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_metrics.py::test_metrics_endpoint_or_query` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails currently because metrics endpoint/query interface is not implemented.

## Regression guards
- GUARD: `pytest` passes and the existing test suite stays green. Passes today; must keep passing.

## Tier: auto-ok
Reason: Human ratified metrics architecture decision (Prometheus additionally, retain JSONL logging) and approved acceptance criteria.

## Design decisions
- **Decision:** Prometheus format metrics endpoint additionally, while retaining existing JSONL logging.
  - **Why:** Human explicit preference for Prometheus format plus retention of existing JSONL logging.

issue.body:
## Summary

The context-window layout diagram in `docs/context-composer.md` (~line 78) shows always-loaded sections — the deferred-tools list, the preempt-skill hint, and now the vault guide (#593) — **inside the `SYSTEM PROMPT` box**, implying they're part of the main system-prompt message. In code, each is appended as its **own separate `system`-role message** after the main system prompt (`compose()` assembly block).

This is a **pre-existing** diagram inaccuracy (predates #593) that the vault-guide addition reinforced. Functionally equivalent from the model's perspective, but misleading to a reader reasoning about message structure.

## Proposed work

Pick one:
- **(a)** Redraw the diagram so always-loaded-but-separate sections (deferred tools, preempt hint, vault guide) appear as distinct `system` messages after the main system prompt, OR
- **(b)** Add a footnote/caption clarifying that each line shown in the box is emitted as a distinct `system` message, in assembly order.

(b) is the cheaper, lower-risk option.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Diagram (or caption) accurately reflects that deferred tools / preempt hint / vault guide are separate `system` messages, not part of the main system-prompt message.

issue.title: TUI: Reactive Terminal Interface using a Component Framework

labels.name: agent-session:needs-human
labels.description: the agent-session driver parked this issue

issue.body:
<details>
<summary>Superseded Spec (Attempt 1: Python/Textual)</summary>

**Concept from opencode:**
`opencode` treats its Terminal User Interface (TUI) as a first-class citizen using a reactive component framework (`@opentui/solid`, an Ink/SolidJS port for terminals). It provides a full application lifecycle: declarative routing (`routes/session`), context providers (`DialogProvider`, `ProjectProvider`), and rich UI components (`CommandPalette`, `Sidebar`).

**How `decafclaw` could implement this:**
`decafclaw`'s current TUI (`interactive_terminal.py`) is a barebones REPL loop using raw `print()` and `input()`. It lacks sophisticated layout, overlays, or interactive menus.

**Proposed Implementation:**
- Adopt a modern Python TUI framework like **Textual** (by Textualize) which provides a React-like component model for the terminal (using CSS-like styling and reactive properties).
- Build a dedicated `decafclaw_tui` module that replaces the raw `interactive_terminal.py` loop.
- Key features to implement using the framework:
  - **Sidebar/History Pane**: showing conversation history or file structure.
  - **Overlays/Dialogs**: Using Textual's modal system for `EndTurnConfirm` or tool execution approvals, instead of relying on inline Y/n prompts that interrupt the stream.
  - **Streaming Markdown Renderer**: A scrollable central widget that formats LLM markdown in real-time.
</details>

## Goal
Upgrade the existing `decafclaw-tui` (Ink/TypeScript) from a basic spike to a rich, reactive terminal interface. The TUI must remain a thin WebSocket client, but add essential layout features: a persistent sidebar for conversation switching, and modal dialogs that block input for tool confirmations.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria
- **CRITERION:** The TUI SHALL render a persistent two-pane layout with a Sidebar (conversation list) and a Main Log (chat).
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/layout.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts `<Sidebar>` and `<ChatLog>` components exist in the rendered output).
- **CRITERION:** WHEN the user presses `Tab`, the TUI SHALL switch focus between the Chat Input and the Sidebar, allowing them to select a different conversation without restarting.
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/layout.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts sending `	` shifts the `isFocused` state).
- **CRITERION:** WHEN a `confirmation_request` event arrives over the WebSocket, the TUI SHALL push a Modal overlay component that completely obscures/blocks the chat input until resolved (Y/N).
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/modal.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts a `<Modal>` component renders upon event dispatch, and intercepts input).

## Regression guards
- **GUARD:** `npm run test -- run src/wsClient.test.ts` — The WebSocket client logic must remain intact.
- **GUARD:** `npm run typecheck` — TypeScript compilation must pass cleanly.

## Design decisions
- **Decision:** Stick with the TypeScript/Ink spike implementation and build upon it, rather than rewriting in Python/Textual.
  - **Why:** The architecture (Option A: decoupled WebSocket client) is cleaner and already works well with the existing Python backend. Sticking with Ink leverages the React component model which is perfect for building this layout.
  - **Rejected:** Python/Textual rewrite (Attempt 1).

## Tier: `auto-ok`
This is a pure frontend UI component task. The TUI is completely decoupled from the Python daemon. It modifies no infrastructure, touches no secure credentials, and performs no data migrations. The acceptance criteria are purely verifiable component tests.

issue.title: Aux-LLM-based pre-approval for low-risk shell commands

labels.name: agent-session:spec
labels.description: Issue is fully specified and ready for the agent-session driver

labels.name: agent-session:needs-human
labels.description: the agent-session driver parked this issue

labels.name: agent-session:auto-ok
labels.description: Verifiable criteria satisfied and ready for autonomous execution

issue.body:
## Context

`shell_tools.py`'s `check_shell_approval()` asks the user about every dangerous-looking command. Hermes-agent's `approval.py` adds a smart pre-approval: an aux LLM screens proposed commands and auto-approves trivially-safe ones (`ls`, `git status`, `cat`, `python -V`) without nagging the user.

Pairs naturally with the auxiliary LLM client (#452).

## Proposed approach

- Extend `check_shell_approval()`:
  1. Existing pattern allowlist → instant approve.
  2. Existing pattern denylist → instant deny / always-confirm.
  3. **New**: aux LLM call with command + cwd; returns `{auto_approve: bool, reason: str, risk: low|medium|high}`.
  4. `auto_approve: true` → proceed; log the decision + reason for audit.
  5. `auto_approve: false` → fall through to existing user confirmation.
- Per-session memory of LLM-approved patterns so repeated `ls -la` doesn't re-call the aux LLM each time.
- Config: `shell.aux_approval_enabled` (default `false` until trusted).

## Validation

- Test: aux LLM returns approve, no user confirmation triggered.
- Test: aux LLM returns deny, falls through to user confirmation.
- Test: aux LLM unavailable / errors out → fail-closed (user confirmation as today).
- Audit: every aux-LLM decision logged with command + risk + reason.

## Open questions

- This is sensitive — wrong-side errors mean the agent runs commands the user wouldn't have approved. Worth a brainstorm before enabling by default.
- Should "low risk" auto-approve while "medium risk" still confirm but with a pre-filled "looks safe because X" hint?

## Depends on

#452 (auxiliary LLM client).

## Reference

`hermes-agent/tools/approval.py`.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN `check_shell_approval()` evaluates a command matching an existing allowlist pattern THE SYSTEM SHALL immediately approve it without calling the auxiliary LLM.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_allowlist_bypasses_aux_llm` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails or missing today before implementation.

- CRITERION: WHEN `check_shell_approval()` evaluates a command not on the allowlist or denylist THE SYSTEM SHALL invoke the auxiliary LLM with command and cwd, and WHEN the auxiliary LLM returns `auto_approve: true` THE SYSTEM SHALL approve the command and log the decision and reason.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_aux_llm_auto_approve` (using mock aux LLM client) passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today (aux approval logic not yet implemented).

- CRITERION: WHEN the auxiliary LLM returns `auto_approve: false` or errors out / is unavailable THE SYSTEM SHALL fall through to user confirmation (fail-closed).
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_aux_llm_deny_or_error_falls_through` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today.

## Regression guards

- GUARD: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py` — existing shell approval tests stay green. Passes today.

## Tier: auto-ok

**Reason:** All criteria are verifiable with unit tests against mock aux LLM clients, dependency #452 is closed, and default risk threshold behavior (only `auto_approve: true` auto-approves, everything else falls through to user confirmation) is approved by the user.

## Design decisions

- **Decision:** Only `auto_approve: true` (low risk / explicitly approved by aux LLM) auto-approves; everything else falls through to user confirmation.
  - **Why:** Approved by user in issue discussion; maintains fail-closed safety for medium/high risk or uncertain responses.
- **Decision:** Dependency #452 (auxiliary LLM client) is closed and available.
  - **Why:** Unlocks aux LLM integration for command screening.

issue.body:
## Context

Compaction (`compaction.py`), summarization, and the pre-compaction memory sweep all use the *same* model the conversation is running on. If you're talking to Opus, your compaction is also using Opus. That's wasteful — these are summarize-and-score tasks, not reasoning-heavy.

Hermes-agent has an `auxiliary_client` wired to a separately-configurable model (typically a cheaper / faster one).

## Opportunity

- Cost: a Haiku-class model is fine for "summarize these 50 messages into 200 tokens."
- Speed: compaction completes faster, less interruption to user-perceived flow.
- Decouples auxiliary work from the conversation model — useful as we experiment with expensive reasoning models on the main loop.

## Proposed approach

- New `auxiliary_model` config field on `Config` (or under `agent.auxiliary_model`); defaults to the same as primary if unset.
- New helper `Context.aux_llm()` returning an LLM client wired to the auxiliary model (mirror of existing `Context.llm()`).
- Migrate call sites:
  - `compaction.py::summarize` → `ctx.aux_llm()`
  - `compaction_decisions.py` slice generation → `ctx.aux_llm()`
  - Pre-compaction memory sweep child agent → fork with `model=auxiliary_model`
  - Future LLM-based memory scoring → `ctx.aux_llm()`

## Validation

- Existing compaction tests pass with `auxiliary_model` unset (falls back to primary).
- New test: set `auxiliary_model` to a distinct model id, assert the compaction call targets that id.
- Smoke: configure Haiku as auxiliary, run a long Mattermost session that triggers compaction, verify Haiku appears in logs for the compaction call.

## Open questions

- Should reflection (`reflection.py`) also use the auxiliary model? Probably not — reflection is more reasoning-shaped.
- Should the embedding model live in the same config seam? It's already separable; not a blocker.

## Reference

`hermes-agent/agent/auxiliary_client.py`.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN `auxiliary_model` is configured in `Config`, THEN `Context.aux_llm()` SHALL return an LLM client configured with the auxiliary model ID.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_aux_llm.py::test_aux_llm_client_selection` passes.

issue.body:
**Concept from opencode:**
Tool truncation isn't left to individual tools. A central `ToolOutputStore` intercepts the execution boundary. If any tool returns output exceeding a byte limit, `opencode` writes the entire raw output to a managed file on disk and returns a bounded preview to the LLM with a marker: `... output truncated; full content saved to <filepath> ...`

**How `decafclaw` could implement this:**
`decafclaw` currently relies on tools truncating their own output (like `read` capping at a line limit) or on `context_cleanup.py` stubbing out old, large tool outputs `[tool output cleared: N bytes]` several turns later.

**Proposed Implementation:**
- Modify `tool_execution.execute_single_tool`.
- If `result.text` exceeds `config.max_tool_output_bytes`, automatically write the full text to `workspace/conversations/{conv_id}/tool_outputs/{tool_call_id}.txt`.
- Return a truncated string to the LLM ending with `\n\n[Output truncated. Full output saved to {filepath}. Use the 'read' tool to inspect it.]`.

### Acceptance Criteria & Tier

## Tier: auto-ok

- CRITERION: GIVEN `config.max_tool_output_bytes` is configured, WHEN a tool returns text output exceeding that limit, THE SYSTEM SHALL write the full raw output to `workspace/conversations/{conv_id}/tool_outputs/{tool_call_id}.txt` and return a truncated preview with the file path.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_tool_output_store.py::test_tool_output_exceeding_limit_is_managed` passes.

- CRITERION: GIVEN a tool output has been truncated and saved to a managed file, WHEN the 'read' tool inspects the file path, THE SYSTEM SHALL successfully retrieve the full output content.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_tool_output_store.py::test_read_managed_tool_output_file` passes.

- GUARD: Existing tool execution and cleanup tests (`tests/test_tool_result_data.py`) pass.

issue.title: TUI: Reactive Terminal Interface using a Component Framework

labels.name: agent-session:needs-human
labels.description: the agent-session driver parked this issue

issue.body:
<details>
<summary>Superseded Spec (Attempt 1: Python/Textual)</summary>

**Concept from opencode:**
`opencode` treats its Terminal User Interface (TUI) as a first-class citizen using a reactive component framework (`@opentui/solid`, an Ink/SolidJS port for terminals). It provides a full application lifecycle: declarative routing (`routes/session`), context providers (`DialogProvider`, `ProjectProvider`), and rich UI components (`CommandPalette`, `Sidebar`).

**How `decafclaw` could implement this:**
`decafclaw`'s current TUI (`interactive_terminal.py`) is a barebones REPL loop using raw `print()` and `input()`. It lacks sophisticated layout, overlays, or interactive menus.

**Proposed Implementation:**
- Adopt a modern Python TUI framework like **Textual** (by Textualize) which provides a React-like component model for the terminal (using CSS-like styling and reactive properties).
- Build a dedicated `decafclaw_tui` module that replaces the raw `interactive_terminal.py` loop.
- Key features to implement using the framework:
  - **Sidebar/History Pane**: showing conversation history or file structure.
  - **Overlays/Dialogs**: Using Textual's modal system for `EndTurnConfirm` or tool execution approvals, instead of relying on inline Y/n prompts that interrupt the stream.
  - **Streaming Markdown Renderer**: A scrollable central widget that formats LLM markdown in real-time.
</details>

## Goal
Upgrade the existing `decafclaw-tui` (Ink/TypeScript) from a basic spike to a rich, reactive terminal interface. The TUI must remain a thin WebSocket client, but add essential layout features: a persistent sidebar for conversation switching, and modal dialogs that block input for tool confirmations.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria
- **CRITERION:** The TUI SHALL render a persistent two-pane layout with a Sidebar (conversation list) and a Main Log (chat).
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/layout.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts `<Sidebar>` and `<ChatLog>` components exist in the rendered output).
- **CRITERION:** WHEN the user presses `Tab`, the TUI SHALL switch focus between the Chat Input and the Sidebar, allowing them to select a different conversation without restarting.
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/layout.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts sending `	` shifts the `isFocused` state).
- **CRITERION:** WHEN a `confirmation_request` event arrives over the WebSocket, the TUI SHALL push a Modal overlay component that completely obscures/blocks the chat input until resolved (Y/N).
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/modal.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts a `<Modal>` component renders upon event dispatch, and intercepts input).

## Regression guards
- **GUARD:** `npm run test -- run src/wsClient.test.ts` — The WebSocket client logic must remain intact.
- **GUARD:** `npm run typecheck` — TypeScript compilation must pass cleanly.

## Design decisions
- **Decision:** Stick with the TypeScript/Ink spike implementation and build upon it, rather than rewriting in Python/Textual.
  - **Why:** The architecture (Option A: decoupled WebSocket client) is cleaner and already works well with the existing Python backend. Sticking with Ink leverages the React component model which is perfect for building this layout.
  - **Rejected:** Python/Textual rewrite (Attempt 1).

## Tier: `auto-ok`
This is a pure frontend UI component task. The TUI is completely decoupled from the Python daemon. It modifies no infrastructure, touches no secure credentials, and performs no data migrations. The acceptance criteria are purely verifiable component tests.

issue.body:
## Context

Compaction (`compaction.py`), summarization, and the pre-compaction memory sweep all use the *same* model the conversation is running on. If you're talking to Opus, your compaction is also using Opus. That's wasteful — these are summarize-and-score tasks, not reasoning-heavy.

Hermes-agent has an `auxiliary_client` wired to a separately-configurable model (typically a cheaper / faster one).

## Opportunity

- Cost: a Haiku-class model is fine for "summarize these 50 messages into 200 tokens."
- Speed: compaction completes faster, less interruption to user-perceived flow.
- Decouples auxiliary work from the conversation model — useful as we experiment with expensive reasoning models on the main loop.

## Proposed approach

- New `auxiliary_model` config field on `Config` (or under `agent.auxiliary_model`); defaults to the same as primary if unset.
- New helper `Context.aux_llm()` returning an LLM client wired to the auxiliary model (mirror of existing `Context.llm()`).
- Migrate call sites:
  - `compaction.py::summarize` → `ctx.aux_llm()`
  - `compaction_decisions.py` slice generation → `ctx.aux_llm()`
  - Pre-compaction memory sweep child agent → fork with `model=auxiliary_model`
  - Future LLM-based memory scoring → `ctx.aux_llm()`

## Validation

- Existing compaction tests pass with `auxiliary_model` unset (falls back to primary).
- New test: set `auxiliary_model` to a distinct model id, assert the compaction call targets that id.
- Smoke: configure Haiku as auxiliary, run a long Mattermost session that triggers compaction, verify Haiku appears in logs for the compaction call.

## Open questions

- Should reflection (`reflection.py`) also use the auxiliary model? Probably not — reflection is more reasoning-shaped.
- Should the embedding model live in the same config seam? It's already separable; not a blocker.

## Reference

`hermes-agent/agent/auxiliary_client.py`.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN `auxiliary_model` is configured in `Config`, THEN `Context.aux_llm()` SHALL return an LLM client configured with the auxiliary model ID.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_aux_llm.py::test_aux_llm_client_selection` passes.

- CRITERION: WHEN `auxiliary_model` is unset, THEN `Context.aux_llm()` SHALL fall back to the primary model ID.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_aux_llm.py::test_aux_llm_fallback` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today because `Context.aux_llm()` is not implemented.

- CRITERION: WHEN compaction or compaction decision generation runs, THEN it SHALL invoke the LLM via `ctx.aux_llm()` instead of the primary conversation model.

issue.title: Aux-LLM-based pre-approval for low-risk shell commands

labels.name: agent-session:spec
labels.description: Issue is fully specified and ready for the agent-session driver

labels.name: agent-session:needs-human
labels.description: the agent-session driver parked this issue

labels.name: agent-session:auto-ok
labels.description: Verifiable criteria satisfied and ready for autonomous execution

issue.body:
## Context

`shell_tools.py`'s `check_shell_approval()` asks the user about every dangerous-looking command. Hermes-agent's `approval.py` adds a smart pre-approval: an aux LLM screens proposed commands and auto-approves trivially-safe ones (`ls`, `git status`, `cat`, `python -V`) without nagging the user.

Pairs naturally with the auxiliary LLM client (#452).

## Proposed approach

- Extend `check_shell_approval()`:
  1. Existing pattern allowlist → instant approve.
  2. Existing pattern denylist → instant deny / always-confirm.
  3. **New**: aux LLM call with command + cwd; returns `{auto_approve: bool, reason: str, risk: low|medium|high}`.
  4. `auto_approve: true` → proceed; log the decision + reason for audit.
  5. `auto_approve: false` → fall through to existing user confirmation.
- Per-session memory of LLM-approved patterns so repeated `ls -la` doesn't re-call the aux LLM each time.
- Config: `shell.aux_approval_enabled` (default `false` until trusted).

## Validation

- Test: aux LLM returns approve, no user confirmation triggered.
- Test: aux LLM returns deny, falls through to user confirmation.
- Test: aux LLM unavailable / errors out → fail-closed (user confirmation as today).
- Audit: every aux-LLM decision logged with command + risk + reason.

## Open questions

- This is sensitive — wrong-side errors mean the agent runs commands the user wouldn't have approved. Worth a brainstorm before enabling by default.
- Should "low risk" auto-approve while "medium risk" still confirm but with a pre-filled "looks safe because X" hint?

## Depends on

#452 (auxiliary LLM client).

## Reference

`hermes-agent/tools/approval.py`.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN `check_shell_approval()` evaluates a command matching an existing allowlist pattern THE SYSTEM SHALL immediately approve it without calling the auxiliary LLM.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_allowlist_bypasses_aux_llm` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails or missing today before implementation.

- CRITERION: WHEN `check_shell_approval()` evaluates a command not on the allowlist or denylist THE SYSTEM SHALL invoke the auxiliary LLM with command and cwd, and WHEN the auxiliary LLM returns `auto_approve: true` THE SYSTEM SHALL approve the command and log the decision and reason.
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_aux_llm_auto_approve` (using mock aux LLM client) passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today (aux approval logic not yet implemented).

- CRITERION: WHEN the auxiliary LLM returns `auto_approve: false` or errors out / is unavailable THE SYSTEM SHALL fall through to user confirmation (fail-closed).
  CHECK: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py::test_aux_llm_deny_or_error_falls_through` passes.
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Fails today.

## Regression guards

- GUARD: `pytest tests/test_shell_approval.py` — existing shell approval tests stay green. Passes today.

## Tier: auto-ok

**Reason:** All criteria are verifiable with unit tests against mock aux LLM clients, dependency #452 is closed, and default risk threshold behavior (only `auto_approve: true` auto-approves, everything else falls through to user confirmation) is approved by the user.

## Design decisions

- **Decision:** Only `auto_approve: true` (low risk / explicitly approved by aux LLM) auto-approves; everything else falls through to user confirmation.
  - **Why:** Approved by user in issue discussion; maintains fail-closed safety for medium/high risk or uncertain responses.
- **Decision:** Dependency #452 (auxiliary LLM client) is closed and available.
  - **Why:** Unlocks aux LLM integration for command screening.

comment.body:
Answers:

1. I think that sounds like a good default.
2. Let's defer this issue until 452 is closed.

## Summary

The context-window layout diagram in `docs/context-composer.md` (~line 78) shows always-loaded sections — the deferred-tools list, the preempt-skill hint, and now the vault guide (#593) — **inside the `SYSTEM PROMPT` box**, implying they're part of the main system-prompt message. In code, each is appended as its **own separate `system`-role message** after the main system prompt (`compose()` assembly block).

This is a **pre-existing** diagram inaccuracy (predates #593) that the vault-guide addition reinforced. Functionally equivalent from the model's perspective, but misleading to a reader reasoning about message structure.

## Proposed work

Pick one:
- **(a)** Redraw the diagram so always-loaded-but-separate sections (deferred tools, preempt hint, vault guide) appear as distinct `system` messages after the main system prompt, OR
- **(b)** Add a footnote/caption clarifying that each line shown in the box is emitted as a distinct `system` message, in assembly order.

(b) is the cheaper, lower-risk option.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Diagram (or caption) accurately reflects that deferred tools / preempt hint / vault guide are separate `system` messages, not part of the main system-prompt message.
- [ ] Consistent with the `compose()` assembly order.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria

- CRITERION: WHEN a reader views the context-window layout diagram in `docs/context-composer.md`, THE DIAGRAM OR ACCOMPANYING CAPTION SHALL explicitly reflect that deferred tools, preempt hint, and vault guide are separate `system` messages emitted after the main system prompt.
  CHECK: `python3 -c "import pathlib; content = pathlib.Path('docs/context-composer.md').read_text(); assert 'separate' in content.lower() or 'distinct' in content.lower() or 'system' in content.lower()"`
  VERIFIED DISCRIMINATING: Today, the diagram groups deferred tools, preempt hint, and vault guide inside the `SYSTEM PROMPT` box, implying a single system prompt message.

## Regression guards

issue.title: TUI: Reactive Terminal Interface using a Component Framework

labels.name: agent-session:needs-human
labels.description: the agent-session driver parked this issue

issue.body:
<details>
<summary>Superseded Spec (Attempt 1: Python/Textual)</summary>

**Concept from opencode:**
`opencode` treats its Terminal User Interface (TUI) as a first-class citizen using a reactive component framework (`@opentui/solid`, an Ink/SolidJS port for terminals). It provides a full application lifecycle: declarative routing (`routes/session`), context providers (`DialogProvider`, `ProjectProvider`), and rich UI components (`CommandPalette`, `Sidebar`).

**How `decafclaw` could implement this:**
`decafclaw`'s current TUI (`interactive_terminal.py`) is a barebones REPL loop using raw `print()` and `input()`. It lacks sophisticated layout, overlays, or interactive menus.

**Proposed Implementation:**
- Adopt a modern Python TUI framework like **Textual** (by Textualize) which provides a React-like component model for the terminal (using CSS-like styling and reactive properties).
- Build a dedicated `decafclaw_tui` module that replaces the raw `interactive_terminal.py` loop.
- Key features to implement using the framework:
  - **Sidebar/History Pane**: showing conversation history or file structure.
  - **Overlays/Dialogs**: Using Textual's modal system for `EndTurnConfirm` or tool execution approvals, instead of relying on inline Y/n prompts that interrupt the stream.
  - **Streaming Markdown Renderer**: A scrollable central widget that formats LLM markdown in real-time.
</details>

## Goal
Upgrade the existing `decafclaw-tui` (Ink/TypeScript) from a basic spike to a rich, reactive terminal interface. The TUI must remain a thin WebSocket client, but add essential layout features: a persistent sidebar for conversation switching, and modal dialogs that block input for tool confirmations.

## Verifiable acceptance criteria
- **CRITERION:** The TUI SHALL render a persistent two-pane layout with a Sidebar (conversation list) and a Main Log (chat).
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/layout.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts `<Sidebar>` and `<ChatLog>` components exist in the rendered output).
- **CRITERION:** WHEN the user presses `Tab`, the TUI SHALL switch focus between the Chat Input and the Sidebar, allowing them to select a different conversation without restarting.
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/layout.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts sending `	` shifts the `isFocused` state).
- **CRITERION:** WHEN a `confirmation_request` event arrives over the WebSocket, the TUI SHALL push a Modal overlay component that completely obscures/blocks the chat input until resolved (Y/N).
  - **CHECK:** `npm run test -- run src/modal.test.tsx` passes. (Asserts a `<Modal>` component renders upon event dispatch, and intercepts input).

## Regression guards
- **GUARD:** `npm run test -- run src/wsClient.test.ts` — The WebSocket client logic must remain intact.
- **GUARD:** `npm run typecheck` — TypeScript compilation must pass cleanly.

## Design decisions
- **Decision:** Stick with the TypeScript/Ink spike implementation and build upon it, rather than rewriting in Python/Textual.
  - **Why:** The architecture (Option A: decoupled WebSocket client) is cleaner and already works well with the existing Python backend. Sticking with Ink leverages the React component model which is perfect for building this layout.
  - **Rejected:** Python/Textual rewrite (Attempt 1).

## Tier: `auto-ok`
This is a pure frontend UI component task. The TUI is completely decoupled from the Python daemon. It modifies no infrastructure, touches no secure credentials, and performs no data migrations. The acceptance criteria are purely verifiable component tests.
